introFa: کتاب «The White Tiger» نوشته Aravind Adiga یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «The White Tiger»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: Chapter 1 ​ "Lord, I feel like a coat hanger," Sally muttered as the camera and lens case edged a little further down on her shoulder. Nothing to do about it; she had her hands full with her carry-on luggage and the drag-behind suitcase. She followed the other passengers out of Customs to the exit, the sign above the door written in Hindi and English, and walked through the automatic doors into the arrival hall. She looked past the eager locals obviously waiting for loved ones and searched the little signs held almost furtively by people meeting unknowns. That was her; unknown, alone in India. Her heart beat too fast. Nerves, that was all. The words 'Tengai Tiger Park' leapt out at her from a sign held by a fellow in a neat khaki uniform but the employment agency had told her she'd be met by somebody and this fellow looked like he was collecting a tour party. She'd come back to him if there wasn't any other option. She glanced further along, letting her eye rest only on signs in English. Ah. 'Dr Sally Carter' hand-printed on cardboard. Wow. The fellow holding the sign was a bit of all right. He topped her five feet eight by a good six inches, wide shoulders and short, black hair. Not a kid, either. He looked about thirty-five; a little older than her. Settle, Sally. He's a man. You're over them, remember? "I'm Sally Carter." She dragged her luggage over to the man and thrust out a hand. She might as well start as she intended to continue, a new doctor, sure, but a friendly one. The man smiled, took her hand while he shoved the folded sign in the back of his jeans. "I'm delighted to meet you, Doctor Carter. I'm Ash." He had a lovely deep voice with barely a hint of that sing- song Indian accent. Her fingers tingled at his touch, like a surge of current that had her heart fluttering. "Sally." "Sally," he repeated. He glanced down at his hand as if he'd felt

something, too, then reached around her for the handle of the suitcase and took the carry-on from her. "Let me take these from you. If you'll come this way, it's a long drive." She admired a tight ass in faded jeans as she pulled the camera and the long lens back up on her shoulder. She could look, couldn't she? Besides, he'd be a driver or something, probably married with children. She hurried to catch up to him, her footfalls echoing on the tiles. "Did you fly direct from Australia?" he asked. "Yes. Singapore Airlines from Melbourne to Mumbai via Singapore, a two-hour wait, then here. About sixteen hours, all up." He maneuvered around a chattering family dawdling toward the terminal's exit. "You'll be tired, then." "Not too bad. I got some sleep. Nice of the raja to fly me business class." The exit doors sighed open. Outside, a cool breeze tingled on her bare arms. She should've taken her jacket out of her bag. Thirty-five in Melbourne to... what?... low teens here? Too late now. She hitched her camera gear up again and followed him to a dusty land cruiser. "Get in", he said, setting her bags in the back. "You can put your camera gear on the back seat if you wish." He swung into the driver's seat and turned on the engine while she dragged her leather jacket out of her bag. "Photography is a hobby?" he asked as he negotiated the traffic to the highway. "Yes. I'm dying to get my first look at a real, live, in the wild, Royal Bengal Tiger. Oh, man, I'll fill an album with shots." "You like tigers?" "Yes. Ever since I was a little girl. I had pictures of tigers all around the walls of my room and that was the first exhibit I'd visit at the zoo." He smiled, watching the traffic, not her. "Wild tigers are magnificent. Nothing like the zoo-bred animals." "No. I hate seeing the big cats in cages. It's sad that it has to be that way to keep them from becoming extinct." He shot her a look. He had those dark, liquid eyes of all Indians but his had a glint, a flash of... something. She gazed at his profile. He was trying hard to be friendly but she didn't think it was natural for him. A bit like her, really, a loner. "Um. You speak English very well."

He grinned, showing even white teeth. "English is a national language in India. We all learn it. Tell me, do you like cricket?" "Oh, well, in Australia you can't avoid it. Bit like here, I suppose." He nodded. "Yes, I do like cricket," she went on. "But not the slap and giggle twenty-twenty stuff. I like test cricket where it's like a game of chess. You know? Tactics and strategy." "So true." He flashed her an approving glance. "Where you need patience and guile, not just explosive flamboyance, although it's good to have that, too." He turned right, off the road from the airport onto a modern, busy expressway. The old roads were still there, though, off to the sides where the locals rode bicycles between fields and rows of houses in various states of repair. She'd been warned about the vast class distinctions in India but it didn't look like she'd get to see much of it on this drive. Feeling a bit like a teenager, she looked sideways at Ash, studying him. He had his eyes on the road; he wouldn't notice her scrutiny. Straight nose, fullish lips. This was one good looking man. He seemed very confident, very relaxed, his strong, well-manicured hands light on the steering wheel, his skin the color of maple. He glanced over at her and smiled. Oh, Lord. As the flush burned up her face, she rubbed her eye to hide her face, her head bowed. When she looked up again, he'd turned away. Might as well watch the scenery. Beyond the confines of a typical modern expressway, successions of small villages appeared between tended fields. Not unlike farmland in Australia, really. After they'd been driving for an hour Ash turned off the highway down an unmade road between the fields. She stretched back in the seat, easing her shoulders and her back. Ash glanced at her, a slight smile curving his lips. He drove with one hand on the steering wheel, the other resting on the door, the vehicle in cruise control. What a hunk. Her mouth positively watered. Slightly curly black hair that reached to his collar, eye lashes a model would kill for. Off limits. He'd probably end up being a patient and a married one, at that. Still, no wedding ring. But maybe they didn't wear wedding rings in India. A village appeared suddenly around the next corner. This was more like the places she'd expected: dilapidated buildings lining a

dirt road, peeling paint, rusting iron, dust. What was this? A crowd of people filled the street ahead, outside one of the shanties, their voices loud and harsh. Raised fists shook. Ash braked and let the car roll to a halt. A man faced the crowd, next to him a woman with her arms around a child who had its head buried in her skirts. The man gestured, open handed, arguing. Someone lunged forward and shoved him, hard enough to have him stagger backwards. The sound of the crowd deepened to a bay. Sally's whole body tensed. This looked ugly. "What's going on?" The man being shoved caught sight of the cruiser and pushed toward it, his arm held out, shouting as he came. "Stay here." Ash was already half-way out the door. He slammed it behind him. Fear trickling down her spine, Sally craned her head as he strode into the mob to meet the fellow, who clutched at Ash's arm, then stepped back. She slipped out of the vehicle. If anybody was hurt, she might be needed. Ash's arrival seemed to have at least stopped the onslaught. The voices faded to a rumbling mutter, then silence. The leader of the crowd made an indignant speech with much finger-pointing at the accused, accompanied by nodding of heads and a susurrus of whispers. Sally edged forward, wishing she could understand the conversation. Ash said a few words, calm, in control. The defendant flung his arms out, made an impassioned plea. She could imagine the 'it wasn't me, I didn't do it'. Derisive cries were flung back but Ash raised a hand and they subsided. She breathed deep, allowing her heart rate to slow. She wouldn't be needed. Ash walked away, back through the crowd to the car. Even before he'd passed, the men let out an exultant shout, surging at the defendant, pushing him into his house. The child cried, the sound piercing over the deeper voices. Shit. Sally strode forward and was jerked to a halt by the hand on her arm. "You cannot interfere." Ash's voice was deep and calm. She spun to face him. "What are you saying? There's a child there. Whatever he's done, the child isn't to blame." "They will not harm the child." "How can you say that?" The men had forged into the house.

Bags and bundles were flung outside, raising dust as they fell in the road. She struggled against his grip. "Let me go. This is wrong." "This is not your concern. The man has broken village law and the family has been evicted." His gaze was blank, impenetrable. When Sally looked back, the woman had staggered out into the street, the child wrapped in her arms. She gazed around her, her face a picture of resignation, then collected up her scattered belongings as best she could while comforting the child. "Why? What have they done?" Sally demanded. "The villagers say he killed a tiger," Ash said. "So? Isn't there a court of law? Shouldn't he be given a trial?" "He has had a trial. Before the village council. And now he has appealed to me." He had to be joking. "You? What are you? The local judge?" He licked his lips. "I am the raja. I'm not a judge but they come to me for advice." Sally's jaw dropped. He was the raja? A part of her realized it made sense. The man had run up to Ash, shouting words which she thought included 'raja'. If that was the case... She leaned toward him. "Stop this, then. Stop it from happening. It's wrong." He glowered down at her. "This is India, Doctor Carter. Not Melbourne. You will please restrict yourself to what you understand." This was wrong, like a lynching in the Wild West. Shrugging his hand off her arm she whirled to stand toe to toe with him. "No, I don't understand. Why don't you explain?" Black eyes stared into hers. She stared back, unflinching, while the hairs stood up on the back of her neck. He exuded menace, as if he held a dangerous beast in check. Somebody else answered her, his tone almost timorous. "The family has been marked. By the Black Tiger." She tore her gaze from Ash to a short man, better dressed than many of the others. "There is a legend," Ash said. "The Tengai forest is protected, guarded by a black tiger. It wreaks vengeance on those who cause damage, especially to the tigers. This house has been marked. The Black Tiger has made its judgment." Oh, what rubbish. Anger bubbling, she glared at him. "So you're throwing these people out because of some superstition?" Ash folded his arms, legs apart. By now many villagers had

surrounded the family. The man had mounted a scooter, his wife and child behind, the people and the machine all festooned with bundles. "The village has evicted them." The other man nodded, his head bobbing up and down. "Mister Murti is the head of the village council," Ash added. "But you're the raja." She pointed a finger at him. "You can stop them." "No. It is their village. I cannot tell them who they must have as neighbors." In the street, the over-loaded scooter gathered speed before a jeering, fist-waving crowd. It was too late now, but even so. This wasn't justice. "Where's the evidence? Who is accusing him?" Ash exchanged a glance with Murti, muttered a few words. Murti beckoned, a wave of his hand. Surrounded by curious villagers, Sally followed him to the front of the shanty, then with mounting curiosity as he walked slowly along the house-front, his head tilted down. He stopped and pointed at a spot just in front of him. "There." Huge pug marks were imprinted in the dirt. Her heart jolted. No ordinary cat or dog could have made these. Three or four of the prints were fairly clear; others had been scuffed or blurred by other traffic. "A tiger's been here? But... how is that possible? Couldn't they track it?" she asked. "You cannot track Black Tiger." Murti's expression was deadly serious, his eyes reflecting awe and fear. "The trail ends and there is no trace of it coming here, or leaving," Ash said. "They followed it in both directions. The beast appears to have circled the house and then..." he opened out his hands, "... disappeared." Blood roared in Sally's ears. "That's not possible." "You can see, here." Murti thrust out a hand, gesturing at the tracks. Around him, others nodded, murmured comments in their language. "The villagers are saying their dogs were barking in the night, then fell silent," Murti added. "They were afraid. No one dared look." "But... but that can't be true. It's just superstition." "Perhaps. But superstition is important in India." Ash waved a hand. "Enough of this. Come. I'll take you home."

Sally took one last, lingering look at the print in the dust. "Yeah. Okay." Ash jerked his head. Back to the car. He strode off, the watchers parting before him. Get a grip. That's what you got in backward, superstitious communities. Or even in advanced, Western societies. Your mother and your brother would've believed this in a heartbeat. A miracle, the work of God. She followed in Ash's wake and jumped into the vehicle. But he —the raja—he wasn't backward. He probably had a university education and judging by that accent, an English university. She still felt stupid at not having realized he was something more than a driver. What had she gotten herself into? Dirt and ignorance and superstition. It had seemed such a good idea a month ago; escape Australia for a year, do some good with the skills she had, forget about David, then go home and start again. Now, what she'd give for a cappuccino in one of the cafés back home in Lygon Street.

Chapter 2 ​ Ash glanced at Sally. She sat tight-lipped in the passenger seat, her knuckles white where she gripped the edge of the seat. Not happy. He could understand her point of view but the poacher had been lucky he hadn't suffered a worse fate. "Huh. You should have killed him." His alter ego's words rumbled in his head. "And have them looking for a man-eater? We've had this conversation." He could hardly explain to her how he knew the man was a poacher. The fool couldn't resist taking a trophy, one claw taken from the body of the tigress. He'd followed the scent and left the tracks around the house himself, knowing the villagers would end the matter without the need for bloodshed. She wouldn't even look at him. Oh, it was probably just as well. The pictures of her Kumar had shown him when he was recruiting didn't do her justice. Short, dark hair that curved around her face, tanned skin and eyes the same dark blue as a baby tiger's. Maybe she had a temper to match. "I like that," the were-tiger said. "What?" "That she has a temper." "Oh, shut up." He glanced at the girl. "I thought tomorrow I'd let you sleep late and conduct short sessions in two villages. But if you feel you need more time..." "That's fine," she snapped "I've worked on less sleep. I'd rather get started immediately." End of that conversation. She turned away from him, gazing out the side window, her body tense. The cruiser breasted a hill and started down into the village of Kinpoor. She sat up, peering through the windscreen. "Are we there, yet?" "Nearly. One more village and then we'll enter the park."

At the outskirts of the township he slowed down and waited while a skinny, slab-sided cow with the typical Brahman hump, twitching ears and sad, soft eyes, ambled out of the way. Sally gazed around her, round-eyed. "Have you been to Asia before?" he asked. She gave the ghost of a smile. "Just ten days in Bali when I was a student." This must be very new, very different for her. The opposite of his own introduction to the world, when he'd left India to study at Cambridge. He'd been miserable until he'd learned to accept what was. He drove on, easing down the street. A scooter carrying a man, and a woman holding onto a child, wobbled past a cart piled high with corn stalks. Scooters and bikes were everywhere, in the road or leaning against walls and trees. Revving engines, beeping horns and the conversation of people filtered through the windows of the car. "It's so noisy. And so many people," she said. "Yes, very different from a modern, Western city like Melbourne. The people have different expectations, different values, too." "Like evicting people over a superstition?" Her voice dripped contempt. He pushed down the tremor of annoyance. He couldn't expect her to understand. "It may have been a last straw, it may have been a vindictive neighbor planting tracks. They may have just had it in for him for some other reason. But it is up to the panchyat—the village council. I have no power there." He pressed his foot on the accelerator as soon as he could. "Besides, are you so sure something like that could not happen in Australia?" "No." She snapped the word without even thinking. "No-one has ever been ejected for being the wrong color, the wrong nationality, the wrong religion?" She sucked in a breath, frowning a little. He must have hit a nerve. Just outside the village, the towers of Tengai palace gleamed white above the enclosing hedge. Twisting in her seat, she stared out the window as they passed. "What's that?" "Tengai Palace." "A palace? Where you live?"

Not likely. Share a wing with his mother? She pried into his life quite enough as it was. "It's a hotel, now." "Oh." She gazed over her shoulder at the receding building. He could guess what she was thinking; was 'home' going to be a hovel? "Don't worry, Doctor Carter, your accommodation will not disappoint. But if it does, room can always be found for you at the palace." Her face flushed. He'd embarrassed her. She was rubbing her thigh, backwards and forwards, backwards and forwards. She stopped abruptly and folded her arms. "Where do you live?" Sally asked. "In the park, the same place as you. But I'm not often here." He slowed to take the right-hand fork down the unmade track between the trees into the forest. "I'm away on business. Making money to keep the park going. And trying to stop tiger poaching." The sunlight had acquired that golden sunset glow, while under the canopy the shadows gathered, preparing for the night. She sat up, staring into the gloom beneath the trees. Probably hoping for a glimpse of a tiger. "Not here. They tend to stay in the centre of the park. Which is good, they're safer." She turned to look at him with those beautiful blue cub's eyes. "Poaching's a problem? Even in the park?" He could drown in those eyes. The steering wheel jerked as the vehicle bucked through a pot hole. He pulled himself together with an effort. "Even in the park. We have prevented most of it here with our constant patrols but even so, a female was killed just recently. If we don't stop it, tigers will be extinct in the wild before the decade is out." The park village appeared between the trees, lights gleaming as the sun sank behind the forest. He drove through the cleared area and rolled the cruiser between the houses, returning waves and wide smiles. Outside a long, modern building set away from the village itself, he halted the car. "This is the clinic and the accommodation block." He swung himself out of the vehicle. In the gathering dusk the chitter of monkeys provided a counterpoint to the trills and chirps of birds settling for the night. He would never tire of this. Far away,

just on the edge of his hearing, he fancied he heard a tiger roar. Welcome home. Sally had clambered out more slowly, wincing a little. Now, she stretched her shoulders and did a few half-squats, then bent her back so her breasts pushed up against her shirt. Her nipples had pointed in the cool air. Lovely body, slim and fit. He looked away, aware of the tingle in his groin. An affair with a foreign doctor wasn't a good idea, especially not so close to his mother. "Raja-sahib?" Ash turned to the attendant who'd come for the bags. "The lady's bags, in the first suite." The man nodded and went about the task. The car door slammed and she joined him, carrying her camera equipment. "I'll show you your rooms and if you find them satisfactory, we'll dine here." She managed a smile. "Of course." She drooped, walking slowly as if reluctant. Was she having doubts? Already? No, perhaps just tired. Something caught her eye and she stopped. She beamed, her head thrown back. He turned to see a peacock, long tail feathers trailing in its wake, silhouetted against the pale orange sky of sunset. "Gorgeous," she murmured. "And my camera's in its case." Stars, she was lovely. He'd like to run his hand through her hair, kiss those laughing lips. He grinned. "They live here. You will see them again. And many other animals." He shed his boots at the door and padded inside in his socks. She hesitated, then kicked off her runners. "Should I always take my shoes off when I go inside?" "It is the custom." In the foyer, he waved a hand at a closed door to the right. "That is the clinic. The sitting room and dining room are through here and the bedrooms are along here." He turned, walked a few paces along a short passage and stopped at a door half-way down. "These are your quarters and further along are mine." The door was open. She stepped inside, her gaze traveling around the spacious double bedroom. "It's nice," she said, laying the camera and the lens on the bed. He hadn't expected anything else. But the bathroom facilities may be a problem. "As promised, the room is of western standards.

You'll find a shower in the ensuite but it's a squat toilet. Do you know what I mean?" He couldn't miss the tiny frown. "I've seen them on TV." "I realize western women find the arrangement... ah... different. But you'll see it's clean and fitted with a hose so you can wash yourself instead of needing paper, which clogs the system. We do not have sewers or septic systems here." "Um, yes, thanks." She dredged up a smile. "I'm sure I'll get used to it." Her ears had gone red. Time for him to escape. "I will leave you, then. You may wish to unpack and shower, maybe look in at the clinic facilities. We eat in an hour. You will not be required to dress formally. Please come through to the dining room when you're ready." One final neck bow and he walked out, closing the door behind him. Stars, why hadn't Kumar found a male doctor? Or one not so damnably attractive? He could lose himself in those eyes. His fingers still tingled from when they'd shaken hands. He felt hot, aroused and gritty. Time for a cooling shower before dinner. PHEW. SALLY PLONKED down on the bed. The room was more than comfortable: spacious, airy, with a built-in wardrobe and a wooden chair and table in the corner. A rug depicting a jungle scene in greens and reds softened the wooden floor and curtains framed glass doors that led out to a verandah facing the forest, now a dark mass in the fading light. Her suitcase stood beside the bed, along with her carry-on bag. So. She'd already managed to have a fight with the raja. At least it sounded like he wouldn't be around all that much. She swallowed the feeling of regret. Yes, he was drop-dead gorgeous but then, that was what she'd thought about David when she first met him. Her vision blurred. She dashed her hand across her face. Oh please, no more tears. Not for that bastard. She'd look to the future, follow her dream of photographing a wild tiger. She opened the suitcase and started putting things away in the wardrobe, mainly jeans, working trousers, shirts and a couple of simple dresses for the hot weather. What should she wear for dinner? Just as well she wouldn't have to dress formally; she'd left

her party clothes at Judy's house. Jeans and a sweat shirt was probably wrong. Wishing she'd taken the time to learn more about this country, she settled on slacks and a long-sleeved blue shirt with a short jacket and fronted up to the dining room. It seemed an acceptable choice. Ash wore black trousers and a white, embroidered shirt that almost glowed against his brown skin. He'd been sitting at the table but rose when she came in. Gee, he was attractive, with that black hair curling around his ears. She'd bet he had a great body, wide shoulders, narrow hips. Her nipples stood to attention, sending a shiver all the way to her groin. Get a grip, Sally. She gazed past him at a large, framed photograph on the wall behind him. A tiger stood on a riverbank, facing the camera, amber eyes aglow, jaw hanging open, revealing a hint of fangs. The sun to the beast's right cast its shadow on the sand beside it, a shadow-tiger, stripeless, stark. For a moment it seemed as if the tiger's eyes met hers, burning into her soul. Her legs trembled. SHE'D GONE WHITE, STARING at him. What had she seen? "Are you all right?" Ash asked, his heart thudding. She jumped, dragging her gaze back to his face. "Interesting picture. Did you take it?" She pulled out the chair opposite him, her chest rising and falling in an altogether too interesting way as she took deep breaths. He sat, suppressing the sigh of relief. She'd been looking at the picture behind him, not him. "No. A professional took it." "It's unusual." She kept her tone light, conversational, but he'd bet her heart rate was above normal. What had she seen in the picture that would affect her so? "She has seen the Black Tiger," the were-tiger muttered. "Stupid. Impossible," he retorted. "Not the best shot of the tiger, though," she continued. "His side's all shaded. If the photographer had taken it from the other side, he would have had the low sunlight right on the hide. Magnificent." He nodded. "He did. We use that shot for our posters for Tengai. But I like this one. It has a different character, another side of the tiger apart from the showy coat." He'd kept it as a joke, really. The shadow tiger, standing there beside the real beast.

Nalini, the young woman who looked after the house, filled the table with a selection of steaming dishes, raita, chappatis fresh from the oven, crisp vegetables and fruit. "Namaskara," she murmured, palms pressed together. "It smells marvelous." Sally smiled at her, a warm, friendly smile. Her shirt gaped a little when she leaned forward, giving a tantalizing glimpse of breast. Forget that. She's Western. He filled Sally's water glass from a jug. "I asked Nalini to reduce the heat of the curries a little for you. I trust it will not be too hot." She took a careful mouthful of a chicken dish. Her eyes widened. He could almost see the sweat gather on her forehead. "It's delicious. A little hotter than I'm accustomed to but that's fine." Her body jerked. Stars, the girl had hiccups, as well as going red. "I get hiccups when the food's too spicy for me. It'll pass." She reached for the water glass. He'd asked Nalini to keep it mild. Any milder and it would be tasteless. "I hope so. This is not especially hot. Eat rice or chappatis to reduce the heat. Water just spreads the burning." Her eyes glinted. "I'll get used to it." She drank a glass of water and poured herself another before he could reach. What could he say? "You'll find the food much hotter in the villages." She flashed a glance at him, bright as laser beams. "I'll get used to it," she repeated She took a deep breath, held it for a few moments, then started again, this time taking more rice and less curry. The hiccups continued, though. She drank a little more water, held her breath again. He couldn't help but stare at her chest. Just the right size, a handful. Not too big, not too small. He forced himself to eat, concentrating on the plate in front of him. What would she think of him? Some sort of sex-crazed pervert ogling her. He looked up and caught her staring at him. Averting her eyes she put down her fork. "I've had enough. I ate on the plane." "Of course." He pushed his plate away. Had she been sizing him up? Judging by that guilty expression, she had. Which still didn't make his thoughts right. Nalini came in, soft-footed, and cleared the plates. The silence grew deeper. She sagged in the chair, obviously tired. What time

would it be in Melbourne? Three, four in the morning? He should let her go to bed. She stifled a yawn "Perhaps you should get some rest." She nodded. "We'll go to the villages tomorrow—after I've shown you tigers." Something to look forward to. Her eyes brightened as she stood. "That would be wonderful." Ash watched her walk away. So easy to picture her naked, with those long, strong legs wrapped around his waist. He rubbed a hand over his face. It had been a long time since a woman had affected him so much. In fact, if there'd been another, he couldn't remember her name. And here she was, in his house, in a room so close to his. Maybe he should go and see his mother. He'd been avoiding the trip and it wasn't late. On the way to the palace he used his cell phone to warn them he was coming. Nasim was waiting, ready to open the door of the car when he arrived. He looked up into a bearded, smiling face. "How are you, Nasim? You have a grandson, I believe?" Ash stepped out of the car and let the man close the door for him. His mother's wing of the palace glowed with soft light. "Yes. Born yesterday. Mother and son are well. But I am very glad you have finally been able to bring a doctor here. My wife and I were both concerned, with our girl so far away in Nagpur." Nasim's boots crunched on the gravel as he led Ash to the side door into his mother's suite. "They are at home?" "Yes. They let her leave when they knew there would be a doctor close by." "I'm pleased to hear that." He was; this was why he'd sought a replacement for Doctor Massud. His people deserved support. Nasim ushered him inside and disappeared. Ash hesitated outside the closed door to the sitting room, straightening his jacket. Best to get it over with. As soon as the door opened his mother rose to meet him, smiling a warm greeting. She wore a pink sari and her arms and fingers sparkled, as always, with gold rings and bangles. The traditional bindi, the red spot on her forehead, matched the sari. He kissed her cheek and caught the fragrance of jasmine, her favorite perfume.

"Asok. It's so lovely to see you. Come, sit down, talk to me." "Have you been well?" Ash said, folding himself into a chair. "Oh, yes. Much better." No, she wasn't. She'd looked away for a fraction of a moment. Perhaps Doctor Sally Carter could persuade her that sometimes Indian traditional medicine did not have all the answers. "Your new doctor is here?" He nodded, accepting a cup of tea from a proffered tray. "She's resting. It's a long flight from Australia." "Any news on who killed the tigress?" He sipped at his tea. "A man from the village. I followed his trail." His mother smiled, cat-like. "Ah. Is he dead?" He shook his head while the were-tiger huffed its contempt. "I left something for the villagers to find so they could confirm their suspicions. He was evicted." She snorted. "Better than he deserved." "Probably. But the point was made. The Black Tiger looms large. It's a wonderful deterrent, most of the time. And as I tried to explain to my soul-mate, if the tiger kills, they search for a man-eater." "The tiger does not have to kill. There are other ways." Her voice was almost a purr. Hire a hitman, she meant. Sure, easily done. His mother could be downright evil. "True. But he may be of more use alive than dead. Kumar is keeping an eye on the man to see where he goes and who he meets." He put the cup on a side table, then refused a refill with a gesture. The servant stepped away. "Be that as it may, the new doctor was not impressed with village justice." He smiled just thinking about her, standing in front of him with her hands on her hips. "She has much to learn. But she's..." Words like beautiful, desirable, sexy crowded for a place on his tongue. "She's a nice lady," he finished. "And she's interested in tigers and tiger conservation." His mother's eyes narrowed. "Not impressed?" How like her to focus on one word. "I think she feared the man's child would be harmed. She doesn't understand how villages work." She'd stood there and glared at him. She had mettle, that one, as well as remarkable blue eyes. "You will have to take her in hand, Asok. Make sure she realizes

her place." Take her in hand. Oh, how he wished. "These things need careful handling. You know how difficult it has been for me to get a doctor here. Besides, it's only for six months until Massud returns." Nasim stepped to her side and leaned over her. "Begging your pardon, Mem-sahib, Mister Gupta has arrived." "Good. Please bring him through." What was this about? He didn't trust that brittle smile, not for one moment. She smiled at Ash as Nasim paced away. "Mister Gupta is a friend staying in the hotel. I said I would introduce you." Nasim returned, bowing in a short, thin man wearing a black dinner suit with bow tie in the best Western style. In contrast his portly wife wore a bright red sari, her collections of bangles, beads and rings out-shining his mother's. A teenage girl trailed behind them. His heart sank. This was going to be another attempt at match-making. Ash exchanged greetings with the parents, trying to ignore the daughter. She looked about fifteen. "I'm honored to meet you, Raja-sahib." Gupta said. He put an arm around his daughter's shoulders and pushed her forward. "This is our daughter, Mahiya. She's our oldest girl—turned seventeen just last month. Say hello to the raja, dearest." The girl gazed up at him, eyes round as a cow's. Hands folded, she whispered, "Namaskara, Raja-sahib." He inclined his head, returned the gesture. Grief, the child looked as though she thought she was about to be ravished. They'd dressed her up in a lovely pale yellow sari, applied rouge and outlined her eyes, festooned her with earrings and bracelets. Did they think he needed the money? Her mother pushed an elbow at her; Mahiya did her best to smile. They sat around a low table in traditional Indian style, the parents with the girl between them, his mother to his right. Servants brought drinks. Gupta wanted to talk finance. And why not? At least the state of the US economy and Chinese expansion were of abiding interest to him, as well. The two women chatted about whatever women chatted about. The girl quickly lost interest in both, sitting with her head bowed, rotating one of the bangles on her wrist. The Guptas didn't stay long. Ash escorted them to the doors so

they could return to their accommodation in the palace. The industrialist would no doubt have been impressed by the sumptuously re-decorated apartment. "Perhaps we can talk again? About...," Gupta jerked his head at his daughter already walking away with her mother. "Some other time." Gupta offered a resigned smile. He'd received the message. Ash returned to his mother, who sat upright, unrepentant, expecting his disapproval, her face set in her usual defiant stare. He dismissed the servants and waited until they'd left the room. "Mother, will you stop playing match-maker without telling me?" He flung himself down onto the sofa. "It's time you married. You're not getting any younger." "She's a child. I'm more than twice her age." She adjusted the sari on her shoulder. "I was married to your father when I was seventeen. It's a good child-bearing age." Child-bearing. It was the only thing she ever thought about. "My father was twenty-eight when you married him. Anyway, things have changed since your day." She pursed her lips, eyebrows drawn together. "It isn't going to happen, Mother. Forget about it. Gupta's just a manufacturer looking for an aristocratic connection. Besides, she doesn't carry the gene." "I thought I'd caught a glimmer." "No." "Are you certain?" He rose to his feet. "Of course I'm certain." He glared at her, sitting there with her chin raised. "My father told me. He said when he met you, he knew. Instantly, with certainty. You spoke to him, connected with him." He pointed a finger at his temple. "Here. With your mind." She sighed. "True." She smiled at something he couldn't see, sad, introverted. "Clear as a bell. You are the one, he said. I still miss him, so very much." She pulled a cushion over, settling herself. "But time is running out and from what I've heard, you've certainly looked. Extensively." He squirmed. It was none of her business. Yet the fact his mother knew of his connection with half the starlets in Bollywood embarrassed him. "You should marry the new woman," his soul-mate purred.

"You should marry a nice Indian girl, Asok. At least the children would have half a chance. You can still have your mistresses on the side." Anger welled. It always had to end this way. Every time. "I don't have any mistresses. I have some girl friends, yes. I'm a man." He stopped his pacing and gazed down at her. "I'll marry when I find the right one. And not before."

Chapter 3 ​ Sally walked along a jungle path, trees crowding on both sides so thick their branches met overhead. The only sound she heard was the soft shuffle of her own footsteps, muffled by undergrowth. Unease started as a prickle in her back, as though hidden eyes watched. She picked up her pace, her heart beating faster, her mouth dry. Cold light shone ahead of her. The moon? The light disappeared, blocked by a huge shape. She halted. Oh God. A black tiger stood on the path, the massive head lowered. Glowing golden eyes glared at her. Her heart pounding, she turned and ran. The beast bounded behind her, the heavy paws thumping on the ground. Thud... thud... She sat up, dripping with sweat, her sheet tangled around her legs. She forced herself to breathe, in through the nose, out through the mouth. A dream, just a dream. She'd often dreamed of tigers, normal, striped ones but she'd never been afraid. A black tiger... just her mind playing tricks. The story in the village, the photograph on the wall, jet lag, tiredness. That was all. She staggered to the bathroom to wipe her face and went back to bed. UNFAMILIAR CALLS AND squawks drifted into Sally's brain. Was that the trumpeting of an elephant? Bright light edged past a gap in the curtains. Beside her on the bedside table the clock's red numbers clicked over to 8:04. Last time she looked it had been ten to three. She must have had some sleep, at least. Scratching her hair, she slid out of bed and padded off to the bathroom. Ash, dressed in jeans and a long-sleeved shirt, appeared in the kitchen at a quarter to nine, just as she was finishing her cereal. "Did you sleep well?" he asked. His smile was enough to make her squirm, even if she didn't like the way he'd treated those people yesterday. The top two buttons of his shirt were undone. Unbidden an image rose in her mind of her

undoing the rest of those buttons, slowly, one at a time. Stop it. "Well enough. It's always hard getting used to a new bed, don't you find?" "No. But then, I travel a lot." He stood beside her, his thumbs hooked into his belt, his fingers on each side of his fly. She couldn't help but look, could she? Judging by the bulge he was pretty well-endowed. "Are you ready to see tigers?" A shiver of excitement of a different kind coursed through her. She bounced to her feet. "Yes, please." He ushered her out the door and led her along a path to a nearby pre-fab with a high, heavy-duty mesh fence defining a large enclosure at its rear. Ash walked beside her, near enough for her to feel his physical presence, hot as a fire. As far as she could tell the yard was empty. Once again, he seemed to know what she was thinking. Her connection to him was nothing short of extraordinary. "Not outside. Not yet." Ignoring the steps he leapt up to the verandah and opened the door for her. The place was fitted out like a laboratory, with stainless-steel benches, a fridge and a microwave along the walls. A young woman came out of a side room smiling a welcome, the stud in her nose flashing as she bent her head over her folded hands. "Namaste, Raja-sahib, Mem-sahib." Sally returned the gesture as best she could. "Namaste." Ash said something to the girl in Marathi and she stepped over to the fridge. Something lay in a pen at the end of the room. Sally's heart jolted. A tiger. It didn't move but two little faces blinked blue eyes and yowled. She melted. Tiger cubs, tiny bundles of striped, tawny fur. Behind her, the microwave started up. "What happened to their mother?" "Shot." He growled the words. His eyes followed her quick glance at the inert body in the pen. "No, that's not her. She was killed and the body taken away. This is a stuffed skin we keep as a simulation. We were lucky the rangers were nearby and they knew she had cubs. These little chaps are only nine weeks old." Poor little things. The girl handed her one of two padded bottles, warm to the touch, while Ash knelt to open the cage. The cubs edged forward, heads waving, sniffing as he reached inside,

making soft huffing noises. They came to him readily, rubbing their heads against his outstretched fist. He lifted the smaller cub out, his expression as tender as a father with a newborn. "This is a little girl," he said, handing the youngster into Sally's eager hands. Oh, gorgeous little beast with enormous paws and white spots on her ears. So cute, so very, very cute. The cub took the teat and drank greedily while Sally cuddled her against her arm, stroking the baby fur. "What will happen to them?" Ash, seated with the male cub, lifted an eloquent shoulder. "They will have to go to a captive breeding program, so we must accustom them to being handled by humans." He looked grim, his mouth a line. He was right, of course. She'd seen the documentaries. Cubs stayed with their mother for as much as two years, learning how to be the jungle's top predator. And tigers didn't live in extended family groups like lions did, so without intervention, they would have died. "Did you catch the poachers?" He raised his eyes without raising his head and for a moment again she thought she caught that dangerous glitter. "The man in the village." A shiver of apprehension slid down her spine. This man exuded... menace? Danger? For a moment it was almost as if darkness drifted around him, like a mist. She shook her head. She was jet-lagged, imagining things. The cub had finished, licking her lips with a pink tongue. Ash let her put them both back, cuddled against a stuffed tiger skin fitted with a hot water bottle and a clock to simulate a heart beat. All because of human greed. Having locked the door behind him he led her back to the house. "That's what this reserve is all about—the tigers. The only thing that can really threaten them is man." He shook his head. "Can you imagine what the Chinese will pay for a tiger corpse? Fifty thousand American dollars, and the price is going up all the time as the numbers of tigers decline. They'll take the skin for coats for rich men's women to wear, grind the organs for some disgusting medication. A pound of powdered tiger bone sells at nearly two thousand US dollars in Hong Kong." His lips curled in a sneer.

"But the Chinese don't catch the tigers; people here do that, peasants who are paid a few hundred dollars. For them, that money is a fortune." They'd reached the veranda to the house. He cleared his throat and pushed the door open for her. When he spoke again, the anger had gone from his tone. "Anyway, what I'm trying to do is improve the lot of the people here, give them health, clean water, jobs, and above all, education. Educated, well-off people like you and me can find room in our hearts to conserve space for the tiger. Poverty- stricken people only have room for the next meal, the next day. That is why you are here, to make a difference to the people's lives." She nodded. So true. She had to admire his thinking, his commitment to the people here and to the tigers. Provided they weren't accused of poaching. Ash drove the land cruiser into the village outside the park. He pulled up outside a new, demountable clinic building and ushered her inside. For a moment his fingers brushed her back, causing a tingle but he snatched his hand away as if he'd been burned. Sally swallowed. He had such an effect on her, more than any other man she'd ever known. Eight women and two men sitting on benches lining the waiting room started to scramble to their feet until he raised a hand and said something. A young woman dressed in a blue nurse's uniform rose from her chair at the reception desk and folded her hands in the now-familiar prayer postion. Sally smiled and returned the namaste. "This is Ela," Ash said. "She'll translate for you and keep records." "Pleased to meet you, Ela. You can call me Sally." She shook her head. "It would not be right, Mem-sahib. The surgery is ready whenever you are." Translate, though? Sally turned to Ash. "I thought everybody learned English?" "Educated people learn English. You'll find most villagers only know their own dialect." He nodded at the girl. "Ela will show you around." "Yes. Yes, of course." Ela escorted her through a door to the surgery itself, neat, clean, with an examination table behind a curtain and a full range of equipment beside a large desk holding a computer. Along a short corridor Ela proudly showed her two small wards, one to each side,

each holding two beds and monitoring equipment. At the end of the passage she opened a door into a simple theatre with X-ray machines and autoclave. "This isn't what I expected," Sally said. "Medical care and education are the most important things we can offer the villagers." Ash leaned against the wall, arms folded. "This is as well-equipped as a small hospital. The other villages are not quite so well-provided but all have a clinic and a school." "That's... excellent," Sally managed. She caught herself staring at him again, imagining him without his shirt. "Well, I'll start on my patients." "Good. When you have finished, please call me on my cell phone. Ela has the number." He walked out between the waiting patients, who bobbed their heads like a miniature Mexican wave as he passed. He certainly had an impact. Maybe she'd been wrong about him. He was a leader, a man who tried to do the best for all his people. Sometimes that meant a few might suffer. A bit like medicine, really. Sometimes all you can do is ease the pain. When the door closed behind him, all faces turned to Sally. She smiled at them. "Well, Ela, let's get started. Who's my first patient?" The morning passed rapidly. Sally fixed a festering sore on a child's leg, carried out health checks on two small children, gave advice on earache and dispensed medication for several minor illnesses. As Ela entered notes onto a laptop, Sally's phone rang. An unfamiliar voice spoke. "Doctor Carter? I am Mister Kumar. We spoke on the video conference. Do you remember?" "I do. Nice to speak with you." She recalled a portly, round-faced man with receding hair, glasses and a friendly smile. His head had waggled from side to side as he spoke. "The Raja-sahib will join us for lunch, but he has some business to finish with the head man. He asked me to fetch you. Are you finished?" "I am, yes." And maybe this was an opportunity to find out a little more about Raja Asoka Bhosle. Kumar arrived at the clinic a few moments later. They exchanged namastes and welcomes, then he said, "It all went well?" "It did." She glanced over her shoulder. Ela still sat at the computer, bent over the keyboard. Sally lowered her voice. "Um... Before we go, can I ask you some questions?"

"Of course." He waited, smiling. She licked her lips. She felt a bit foolish about this, but if she didn't ask she wouldn't know. "Mister Kumar, the raja lives in the park. I'm sorry if I sound nosey but I don't want to make mistakes when speaking with him. Is his wife deceased? Does he have children?" Kumar chuckled, his eyes sparkling behind his glasses. "He has never married. His mother has almost despaired of him. Even now she will still try to arrange a marriage for him. As for children..." he smirked, "...none that I know of." Rich, handsome. Another playboy type. Like David. For a moment her ex's face rose in her mind, the way his blue eyes crinkled when he smiled, that lock of hair that kept falling over his forehead. "His father is dead?" "Yes. Killed in a traffic accident in Mumbai many years ago, now." Kumar fidgeted. "Is there anything else?" "Yes. I heard a story in the other village, about a black tiger. What do you know about that?" He chuckled, shaking his head. "I've heard the story. The Black Tiger that haunts the jungle." Rolling his eyes he hooked his fingers into claws for a moment. "I accept it has to be just a story but they all seem to believe it." The beast from her dream rose in her mind, the terror gone in the bright light of day. He nodded. "Oh, yes. The poor, the uneducated. I'm not from this area but tales like this abound in India. It is part of tradition, of culture. I smile and I accept. It's wisest. And now, perhaps we'd better go." He ushered her out the door. "Everyone wants to meet you. We will be having lunch with the police inspector, the head man and the members of the village council." She suppressed the sigh. She hated gatherings, parties, socializing. But it had to be done. They sat her next to the raja, in a position of honor. She smiled until her jaw ached, nodded, explained she came from Melbourne and how happy she was to be here, even talked a little about cricket. Food was served without knives and forks. Ash bent toward her, his voice lowered to a whisper. "Let me select the curries for you."

She watched him load a platter for her. "Scoop the food with the naan bread," he said, handing her the dish. His hand brushed hers, sending a rush of warmth to her face. "Do not use your left hand. And don't forget, use lots of rice to reduce the heat of the curry." She nodded, trying to still the pounding of her heart. He leaned over her, his breath warm on her cheek. She gazed into dark, slightly worried eyes. "Thank you. I'll be fine." Now to hope it wasn't so hot she couldn't cope. She torn off some bread. "Now rice, then some curry," he said. They were all watching her. Rice, then a tiny bit of the lentil curry. He nodded, a smile in his eyes. It was hot but the bread and rice helped. She ate enough to be respectable and managed to avoid the hiccups. So far, so good. He'd kept an eye on her throughout the lunch, making sure she was comfortable. She knew rajas no longer had any official status in India but Ash was clearly held in high esteem. Everyone was polite and attentive, asked his opinion and although he spoke with the locals he took time to speak with her, too. He made her feel special. For the first time in a long while. After lunch Sally, Ela, Kumar and Ash climbed into his land cruiser and drove out of the village, avoiding dogs, bare-footed, tousle-haired children, chickens and a cow. "The next village is Sanchin, where we had the small fuss yesterday." Ash slowed down for an ox-drawn cart piled high with grain. Not far away, over the fields, the jungle formed a dense, dark line against the bright blue sky. "I have not made as much progress there, yet. But there is a sealed well, and now a small clinic." They drove down the street, loud with scooters, goats, dogs and people. Gap-toothed women smiled and waved, bangles flashing in the sunlight. Squealing children played in the dirt. So different from the baying mob of yesterday. They drove past the house where the poacher had lived. It looked like somebody else had taken up residence. So unfair, taking away what little those people had. Even if he was a poacher. She imagined she heard a growl that almost turned into words. 'Deserved.' She glanced at Ash and Ela. "Did you say something?" They shook their heads. Ash deposited her with Ela outside the clinic, Mister Kumar took her place in the front passenger seat and the cruiser drove on. "This is not as fancy as the one in Kinpoor," Ela said, unlocking

the door. "It has no wards, just a surgery." She held the door to the demountable open. Sally climbed the short flight of steps into the waiting room. Three women followed her in, one of them holding a baby, another's bulging belly advertising her pregnancy. Sally waved a hand, inviting them to sit on the benches. "Tell them I'll be ready soon." She walked through to the surgery, laid out exactly as in Kinpoor, and dropped her treatment bag next to her desk. Ela brought in the first patient, the young, pregnant woman, who offered her a shy smile. She and Ela exchanged a barrage of Marathi involving a lot of nodding. "She has been to the birthing woman here but she wants to check with a Western doctor to be sure," Ela said. Sally took blood pressure, listened to the infant's heartbeat and let the woman use the stethoscope so she could hear, too. The beaming smile was sufficient reward; Ela had to listen, as well. More patients had arrived. Sally worked through them methodically, taking samples for tests in some cases, dispensing medication for others. A child of about six came in, carried by an anxious mother. Sally caught the sour stench of vomit as soon as they entered the room. As she took the child's pulse and temperature, Ela conducted the usual conversation in Marathi, translating Sally's questions. Were the child's stools normal? When had the condition begun? Had she eaten anything bad? Did the siblings have the illness, or the parents? Something angered the woman; she answered with a curled lip, eyes blazing hatred. "What?" Sally wished she could understand the language. "I'll explain, later, Mem-sahib," Ela replied. "It's not medical. It's about what happened yesterday. She says it was the family's fault. They called the Black Tiger and brought disease." Sally let it go. Ela was clearly nervous, chewing her lips. "Well, tell her that her child very likely has a virus. She should make sure the little girl has lots of water—but it has to be boiled, then cooled, first. When she can eat, give her small meals of rice. If she's not much better tomorrow, have someone call me." A few more words with Ela, a murmured namaste and the woman left the room. Sally flopped in her chair. "And what did you think of that? The

Black Tiger bringing disease?" Ela fidgeted, shifting her weight from foot to foot. "It's tradition. I don't know much about it, just that the tiger guards the forest. The woman just now, she was sure the man they drove out was a poacher and they were being punished for shielding him." "Okay." What could she say? The child would probably be fine tomorrow and then the woman would say it was because the poacher had been driven out. Stupid superstitions. She finished the surgery, then called Ash. He asked her about the surgery and what she'd accomplished. She finished with the vomiting child. After they'd left Ela and Mister Kumar in Kinpoor, she said, "Look, I'm still concerned about that family in Sanchin—" "The poacher?" "Yes. He has a family. They'll suffer." He made a cutting gesture with his left hand. "He is a poacher. Do you know what they do?" The menace in his voice sent a chill down her spine. "They kill tigers." "They don't just kill them." He drew in a deep breath. "It isn't pretty. They'll use guns if they have them. If they haven't, they'll use snares or dig a pit or leave out poisoned meat. Often the beasts die in agony." "Errk. Poison baits? I thought tigers were hunters." She recalled her girlfriend's contorted face as she told the story of her dog, poisoned in her back yard, convulsing in pain, thrashing before it finally died. He wrenched the steering wheel around to park outside the house, sending up a cloud of dust. Glaring at her, he opened the car door. "Tigers are pragmatic. Why hunt if food appears? They'll take another animal's kill. All a poacher has to do is know the forest, where the tigers travel, where they hunt." Lord, what had she triggered? He stomped up the steps, kicked off his boots and waited for her just inside the door. In the living room he set up his laptop on the table and pointed a finger at a chair. "Let me show you how poachers work." This wasn't going to be pretty. Sally moved reluctantly to stand beside him, as a picture loaded. A dismembered carcass, the striped hide smeared with blood. They'd cut off the paws, pulled out the claws. Brown stains caked the ground. Sally pulled over a chair and

sat as he moved through the album, showing picture after disgusting picture. Tigers impaled, butchered, strung up, slaughtered. She'd seen a lot in emergency at the hospital but this... this was torture, cruelty of the worst kind. "And all done by people," she murmured. "Greed." He turned to her, his gaze intense. "Do you still feel sorry for poachers?" What could she say? "Not for people who do this." He switched off the laptop and leaned back in his chair. The rage had dissipated, the tension draining from his shoulders. "I'm sorry. I feel so strongly about this. The tigers are my life." She wanted to reach out and touch him but the gesture seemed too intimate. "I can see that. But what can you do to stop the poachers?" Her words sounded lame. "Try to stop the pushers. It's like drugs, d'you see? Somebody, somewhere, benefits from this. If they don't buy, the tigers will not be killed." She nodded. "Chinese medicine. But it takes a lot to change traditional beliefs." He arched an eyebrow. "So very true. The Chinese Government claims to be trying to change peoples' perceptions. Our Government has protection programs and tiger reserves. But how much of it is lip service and will it be enough?" He shrugged. "We patrol and we educate and I try to improve the lot of the villagers near the reserve here." "Can't the police do anything?" "Wild animals are not high on their list of priorities." He smiled and she found herself leaning toward him, sucked into the deep, unknowable darkness of his eyes. His voice deepened. "For me, the tigers are everything. I will do what I can because I must."

Chapter 4 ​ Ash parked his car at Tengai palace and bounded up the steps into the foyer, where Kumar waited for him. Judging by the look on the man's pudgy face, he wouldn't have good news about the accused poacher. Inside Kumar's office, Ash said, "Did you find him?" Kumar went around the desk and sat, his expression rueful. "We found him, yes. Needless to say he denied doing any sort of poaching, claimed he'd found the tiger claw in the park." Ash snorted. "It was fresh." "Yes, but it's possible. They lose claws sometimes when they fight, don't they?" True. But he could hardly tell Kumar how he knew where the claw came from. "Surely there's more." Kumar raised his hands, arms outstretched. "We offered him a thousand rupees to tell us who he worked with. He said two other men he didn't know took the body in a truck fitted with a crane. He didn't see the number plate." "He must have worked through somebody." "Oh yes." Kumar's head bobbed up and down. "But the name matches hundreds in Mumbai." Damn damn damn. "So nothing. Again." Ash dashed a hand through his hair. "Where has he gone?" "To live with relatives in Mumbai. We're keeping an eye on him." "What's the address?" Kumar's eyebrows arched. "No address, Raja-sahib. The slums of Mumbai, people disappear." "But you're having him watched?" "Well... yes. One of my people there." "Good. Give me his cell phone number." The manager scratched his nose. "Sir... we have it under control." "Give me the number." It was stupid. But he was sick of doing

nothing, getting nowhere. Showing the pictures of slaughtered tigers to Sally last night had only inflamed his anger. "We should have killed him," growled the were-tiger. Kumar shrugged, looked up a listing on his computer. Gazing at Ash over the top of his glasses, he read out a number. Ash typed it into his cell phone. "What will you do?" Kumar asked. "I'll contact him this evening or tomorrow. I get so tired of doing nothing, getting nowhere." "So true." He gazed at Ash. "I know it is important to you but I feel what you do for the villagers here, providing education, a doctor, that is much more beneficial." "Sure." Ash rose to his feet and shoved the cell phone into his pocket. A doctor. Doctor Sally Carter. Blue eyes like a tiger cub's. After they'd talked about poaching they'd watched TV for a while. He went to his room early, pleading work. Anything to get away from her, stop himself from touching her. A wave of longing swept through him. Strange how quickly he'd connected with her. "Not strange at all," the were-tiger said. "It's impossible. She can't have the gene," he snapped. "I'm off. The helicopter will be waiting." Kumar folded his hands. "Namaste. I look forward to your safe return." ASH REFUSED DINNER with the financiers in Mumbai and rang Kumar's contact on the way back to his hotel to set up a meeting. He changed into jeans and caught a taxi to an address in the Mumbai suburb of Dharavi. He almost gagged as the stink hit him when he stepped out into the street. Mud, excrement, rotting waste. Revolting. "Wait," he told the driver, slipping him a one hundred rupee note. "I'll make it worth your while." The man took the note but shook his head. "I come back. You call me." He brandished his cell phone. Ash entered the number and went to look for his contact next to the entrance to a church. A beggar hobbling on a makeshift crutch thrust out a filthy hand and he dropped coins for him. Care-worn women eyed him. A man bumped into him and apologized profusely but Ash thrust out a hand and grabbed the urchin trying to steal his wallet. The girl

cringed, huge dark eyes pleading. She'd probably learned how to act remorseful and cute from the same person who taught her how to steal. Feeling like a fool, he gave her five rupees and sent her away. "You should be careful. They'll all want some." The voice didn't match the man's appearance. He wore a grubby dhoti with an equally grubby shirt and smelled as if he hadn't had a bath in a month. At least he blended in well with the locals. "You know where he is?" Ash asked. "I want to talk to him." The fellow shrugged. "As you wish." He looked Ash up and down. "But take care. They don't like tourists here." "Don't worry. I can take care of myself." In his mind the were- tiger unsheathed its claws enough to show the tips, then withdrew them again. Excitement tingled his nerves. Danger was thrilling, always had been. Allowing his tiger persona to slip a little way across into his human form—just enough to heighten his senses but not change his appearance, he followed his contact into the reeking lanes between the shanties. "The place stinks," the were-tiger complained. Rotting garbage, urine, and decay competed with the smell of unwashed bodies and the cloying odor of the nearby marshes. Eyes watched him pass. He caught the glint of a knife. The were-tiger pressed at his mind, eager, ready. His contact slowed and gestured. "There." Ash recognized him at once, the man from Sanchin, obvious in his too-clean western trousers. He stood outside what passed for a shop here, laughing with another man. The laugh vanished when he caught sight of Ash. He ran. "Ah. A hunt." Ash forced the were-tiger back as the adrenalin surged through his body. He couldn't change here, couldn't let the beast appear but he could use its strength for a chase. He leapt after the poacher, leaving Kumar's contact in his wake. Legs pumping, the prey dodged down a side alley pushing aside a man who tried to intervene. Ash closed the distance, leaping over the fallen man. Another corner. The ground rumbled and a deep, throbbing blast of sound to the left almost deafened him. A train, not yards away, easing through a narrow corridor between the shacks. People jumped out of the way but the fugitive spurted, crossing the tracks inches in front of the engine. Ash skidded to a halt, watching the horrified driver mouthing imprecations from his seat.

Damn. He'd never catch the fellow now. "I told you we should have killed him," the were-tiger growled. Perhaps he should have. But killing was too easy, seductive, a siren-song that rippled through his muscles. He wondered if the British police had ever solved that mysterious death years ago near Cambridge, where a gang of young bullies, mad with fear, had claimed something had killed their mate. Well, they had tried to mug him, a lone Asian outsider, four of them, armed with knives. He could easily conjure up the smell of blood, the taste of it dribbling down his fangs and into his mouth. The exaltation replaced by the guilt as he threw up into a drain. The train rattled on, a parade of dilapidated carriages over-filled with passengers, faceless people going to unknown places. "Not much chance of seeing him again." His contact appeared beside him, breathing heavily. "You sure can run." The guard's van rumbled past, disappearing between the rusting shanties with a trailing blast of sound. With the train gone, people wandered back out onto the tracks. On the other side a few people bent over a prone body. Somebody was pulling off the western trousers. Ash bounded across. The looter stood his ground until Ash stared at him. Even then, he only retreated to the loose circle of curious onlookers. The scent of blood, rich and thick, twitched in Ash's nostrils. He mashed his lips, willing the bloodlust away. The were-tiger growled. "It should have been us." Kumar's contact bent beside the body lying face down in the mud. "His throat's been cut. Probably for his clothes. His boots are already gone." He flipped the body over, exposing the oozing slash across the victim's throat. The blood had mingled with the mud. Damn it. Ash scrubbed his chin with his fist. So near and yet so far. But then, could the fellow really have told any more than Kumar had related? He turned away, back toward the haven of the main road. "What about his family? Have you talked to the wife?" he asked. "I haven't." "Take me there." He had to duck his head to get inside a hovel dark and noisome as a cave, the dank walls leaning drunkenly. Two women, both with children peering around their skirts, gazed at him, eyes wide. The

poacher's wife murmured namaste, her expression a mix of fear and resignation. Ash sent the others out and told her about her husband. Her face crumpled, tears streaming down her cheeks. "I told him," she said between sobs. "Told him it would lead to ruin. And now this." "Did he tell you who he talked to about killing the tiger?" She shook her head, dabbing her eyes with the edge of her sari. "He came home all happy, showed me money. I asked what for but he wouldn't tell me, just said we'd be rich." "How much money?" "I'm not sure. And then we were thrown out of the village." Seeing her here, in this squalor, he felt bad. But the man had been a poacher. "We were going to move into a house tomorrow. He said this morning he would be given five thousand rupees and then we could go, live somewhere nice." Her voice faltered as she subsided into sobs. Ash put out a hand. "He was to receive more money? Here?" She nodded, still sobbing. "Do you know who?" But her husband had not confided in her. He stood, remembering only just in time to keep his head down. Shanties were not built for men as tall as him. He pulled out his wallet, leafed out five bank notes and held them out for her. "For you and your little girl. Go somewhere decent." Her eyes widened, lips parted in a silent O. Five thousand rupees was pocket money for him. For her, it was a fortune. He pushed out of the shack, her namaste ringing in his ears. As soon as he could, he rang for the taxi to get him out of this stinking mess. The first thing he'd do was shower.

Chapter 5 ​ Sally kicked off her boots on the veranda and padded inside in her socks. The day had sped by, filled with noise and people. She dumped her medical bag, changed into jeans and headed for the kitchen. What she needed right now was a cup of tea. Seated at the bench in the kitchen, she drank. Lord, it was quiet here. Maybe she could turn on the TV, just to have some voices? Admit it. You miss him. She did. He'd been gone for a week now and he wouldn't be back for a few more days. Even visits to the tiger cubs weren't the same without him. She ran a hand back through her hair. She could not afford to let him get under her skin like this. It would only end in hurt. Hers. She drained her tea and ran water in the sink to wash the cup. The door bell rang. She straightened. The girl, Nalini, wouldn't have rung the bell. Perhaps this was an emergency. Drying her hands on a cloth, she went to the door. A middle-aged man stood on the veranda, smiling. "I'm Doctor Carter. Can I help you?" "Oh, no problem, Doctor," he said in excellent English. "I'm Haji Rao, the local school teacher. I thought you might be lonely and maybe would like to visit my wife and me. We have a house in the village." "Come in." She stepped aside, aware of the dishcloth dangling from her hand. "No, no. I'm sent to ask you to come to our house to share a meal with us." "Gosh. Thanks. Thanks so much. That would be lovely." "This evening? If that suits? Tomorrow, of course, if you have something else planned?" She grinned. "No. I've nothing planned. I'd love to come." "Good. I will return a little later." One last smile and he stepped

off the veranda, striding in the direction of the village. Fantastic. Sally's spirits soared. Maybe she could make some friends here, get to know a few people, learn some of the customs. "THIS IS SO KIND OF you, Mister Rao," she said when he returned for her. "Haji. My wife imagined it would be strange for you, alone in the house with the raja away." She matched his stride; Haji wasn't as tall as she was. "I value the opportunity to meet some new people, perhaps learn a little about how you live." "Very different to you, I expect." He nodded a greeting to a passing man leading a cow. "I have seen on TV. You have large houses in Australia." He guided her to a single story house surrounded by a veranda, not dissimilar to the building she lived in herself. "It is prefab," he said proudly, holding the front door open for her to pass through. "The raja has provided good houses here, which will withstand the monsoon. And we even have three bedrooms. Luxury." Sally stepped into a living room where polished brass ornaments on carved wooden tables glinted in the light. Woven rugs provided color. A small, smiling woman who had to be Haji's wife bowed to greet her with the now-familiar namaste. A boy and girl stood on each side of her, shy but curious. They looked about ten or twelve years old. To her surprise, Haji didn't introduce his family, but guided her over to an old woman seated in a cane chair, her wrinkled face screwed up into a toothless smile. "This is my mother." "Namaste," Sally murmured. The old lady looked about ninety. Those wise old eyes, half-hidden in folds of flesh, gleamed with intelligence. Haji poured out a torrent of rapid Marathi, which the old lady acknowledged with a few words. "She does not speak English," Haji said. "She greets and welcomes you." "Tell her 'thank you'," Sally said. Now Haji turned to his family. "This is my wife, Divya, my son, Ali, and my daughter, Nasmi."

They murmured greetings, all in English. Sally responded in kind, with a namaste and 'good evening'. "Thank you for having me, Divya. I'm honored." "They will speak English while you are here. It's good practice for them," Haji said. Divya and Nasmi disappeared through a door while Haji settled her on a cane chair. He and his son sat on a low bench opposite. "Is your mother ill?" Sally asked. Haji shrugged. "She is old. Her body is weak but her mind is not." No. That was common enough. The women returned with tea, its fragrance filling the small room. Divya served her mother-in-law first, setting a cup near to her hand. Extended family, lovely to see, the younger generation caring for their parents. That wasn't going to happen in Sally's family, ever. The evening passed quickly after the initial awkwardness was overcome. Haji explained customs, the children asked questions. Haji made sure his mother was involved by translating. The old woman responded with nods, smiles and a few comments of her own. "I wish I could speak a little of your language," Sally said after Haji had translated for his mother. "What's the word for 'tiger'?" He told her and helped her to get the pronunciation right. "How is it written?" she asked. He wrote the symbols, explained a little of the alphabet. "Haji, could I pay you to give me lessons? Teach me your language?" Haji's eyebrows shot up. "You want to learn Marathi?" "Yes. I have Ela to translate but even a little helps. Perhaps I could visit once a week or something and you can teach me some words? I'll pay, of course." "It would be my pleasure. But I will not accept payment." He shook his head. "Oh, no no no. But if you would keep an eye on my mother's health I would be grateful." "Of course. And yours and Divya's too." She hesitated. Could she ask him? Why not? He could only say 'no'. "Could I ask you something? What can you tell me about the Black Tiger?" The school master leaned back in his chair and pushed his

glasses up his nose. "You have heard of the Black Tiger?" "Well, yes. A family was driven out of a village because they'd upset the beast. Hadn't you heard?" He shook his head. "We do not hear about what happens in other villages, Doctor Sally." No, of course not. It wouldn't be any different at home. You only ever learned about things if they were reported in the papers. She explained to him how the family was evicted. "I saw the tracks. Massive pug marks in the dirt that didn't go anywhere. But that's impossible. I asked about it, but everyone just said it was a legend that the villagers believed, a religious thing." Haji nodded. "That is so. In India, Hinduism is the main religion, as you know, but Hinduism incorporates elements of animism, a belief in animal spirits and the power symbols of the natural world. One such is Ganesha, the elephant god. You have seen our temple to him. But here in this village, our real god is the tiger. In Tengai, the tiger is the protector, the guardian of the forest and we protect him." "And this Black Tiger that is supposed to have driven the man out, is it some mythical being?" "Yes." "But surely you don't believe in something like that?" He wobbled his head from side to side, a caricature of an Indian. She suppressed the desire to laugh. "The educated part of me says no, I do not. Yet I have heard stories, handed down. I've lived around here all my life, you see," Haji said. "I've heard the tales the mahouts tell, of a great beast that tears out the throats of those who kill the tigers. All over India the rulers were the only ones allowed to hunt them. That is why they are 'royal'." He wagged a finger, waving it from side to side. "But not here in Tengai. The rajas never hunted tigers." He smoothed down his mustache with one finger. "In this modern day it is a story used to scare children. If you do wrong, the Black Tiger will come to take you away. Don't stray into the jungle at night." "I can't imagine you'd need stories like that, what with leopards, bears, jackals, wolves and ordinary old, stripy, savage tigers to contend with. Not to mention cobras and scorpions." He frowned, his face serious. "No, this is not an ordinary animal, you see. India has were-tigers, like your European werewolves, a

man who is also a beast." Oh, this was ridiculous. "So I need to take care at the full moon?" "No, actually. The were-tiger is able to change shape at will. This house you spoke of ... the were-tiger could approach as a man, change to leave the pug marks, then change back to a man again. There could be such a beast walking amongst us. You could not tell." He was deadly serious. A shiver slithered down Sally's spine. This story must run deep, like the tales of vampires in Transylvania. She stood. "Thanks, Haji. How do I say that in Marathi?" He told her, then she repeated the words. He smiled. "You are a good pupil, Doctor Sally." He folded his hands. "Namaste." She walked home through the village. One of these people, a were-tiger? She dismissed the notion. It was impossible. Yet she would be foolish to underestimate the importance of belief. When she did psychology classes in medical school the prof had told a story of an aboriginal community where the witch doctor had carried out the 'pointing the bone' ceremony on a man. The victim believed he was cursed and he died of no obvious physical cause. What went on in a person's mind was just as important as their body. For that matter, what about what went on in her mind? Had she dreamt of a were-tiger? She stopped in front of the photograph hanging on the dining room wall, its body outlined in gold. She shook her head, shaking away the idea. It couldn't be, just... couldn't be.

Chapter 6 ​ She wasn't home when Ash arrived at his quarters in the park. He couldn't help the little flare of disappointment, even if he hadn't expected her to be there. It had been two weeks since he'd last seen her. He took off his jacket and threw it over a chair, then tugged at his tie and unfastened the top two buttons of his shirt. Ties. Stupid western inventions. He glanced at his cell phone. He could call her. No. He'd been through that a dozen times already. She was here to work and he couldn't afford an affair. Especially under his mother's nose. Stars, how would Sally take having to go with him to meet his mother this evening? He had hoped Kumar could have done the introduction. But no, that wasn't good enough for mother. He would have to introduce the new doctor to her himself. Might as well check some figures while he waited for Sally. He sat at the dining table and opened his laptop. He'd read the same column of numbers three times when he heard the deep rumble of the land cruiser pulling up. The noise stopped, the car door clunked shut and footsteps clacked on the veranda. He turned to face the doorway when she came through. She wore tailored pants and a blue shirt that matched her eyes and her face flushed as she smiled. "You're back." He rose to his feet, fighting the urge to take her in his arms. The shirt was unbuttoned enough to show a tantalizing glimpse of cleavage. His heart beating too fast, he dragged his gaze away. "I am. How was your day? Kumar tells me you're doing well in the villages." She shrugged, smiling. "I've heard there have been some complaints from the men about the foreign female doctor." "I wouldn't expect anything else. It's more important to me that you're improving the lot of the women." He waved a hand. "Please, sit down. Would you like tea?"

"Yes, tea would be nice Look, do you mind if I change first?" He grinned. That might mean something different if she said it to him. "I assume you mean your clothes." He'd better get it over with. "Before you do that, I hoped you would come with me to dinner tonight." Her face lit up. "Sure. Where are we going?" Damn. She'd misunderstood, no doubt expecting some romantic, intimate interlude.
