He'd prefer that. "My mother wishes to meet you in her apartments at the palace. She's asked us to dine with her." She sagged, the smile fading from her lips. "That'll be fine. What should I wear?" He'd messed that up. He felt like a floundering teenager. "My mother is conservative. Do you have a dress?" She nodded. "When do we leave?" "Six? She's excited at the prospect of meeting you, asked me when I spoke with her earlier today to bring you." "I'm sure it'll be lovely to meet her, too." She worked hard at a smile. She seemed to have recovered, accepting the engagement as necessary. "We have some time," he said. "Show me your photos? I'd love to see them." He dragged a chair round to sit beside her, never touching but very close. He caught a glimpse of white lace underneath the shirt. She wore no makeup, and simple stud earrings in her ears. He longed to tuck the errant strand of hair behind her ear. "You're very good at photography," he said. "You've captured so much of the essence of this place. Kids playing cricket, the elephants bathing, the school." She turned to him, wafting a hint of lavender from her hair. "It's a way for me to turn off, think about something other than being a doctor. Don't you get sick of traveling?" "I do. Soon, I won't have to go away so often. I should be able to let things run by themselves, with me controlling from here, via the net." He stretched, arms behind him, back arched. "I'm off to shower and change." Before he changed his mind and did something he might regret. He stood and caught her looking at him, her eyes roving over his body, her pupils wide. Pushing the chair away from the table she cleared her throat. "Me too."

If he wasn't mistaken, she was as attracted to him as he was to her. He felt hot. It had better be a cold shower. He was ready before her, of course. He'd dressed for the occasion, cream trousers and long, embroidered jacket with a high collar. He turned when he heard her footsteps. She wore an ankle length cream dress with a close-fitting, embroidered bodice that scooped across the top of her breasts. Sapphire stud earrings glinted in her ears and she'd used enough makeup to accentuate her eyes and her lips. She looked gorgeous, delectable. "We match. You look lovely." Smiling, she caught her lip in her teeth. "I hope your mother will approve. I didn’t bring much of a wardrobe with me." How could she not approve? He shepherded her toward the door. "We shall see." And then they could come back to the park and spend some time together, perhaps. "Why don't you live at the palace?" she asked as he drove. "Too formal, too claustrophobic. And no privacy. Especially now it's a hotel." The palace sparkled in the night, its newly-painted walls gleaming in uplights set at the base. Inside the gates a low fence lined a formal garden within the confines of a circular driveway. She glimpsed clipped plantings and paving around fountains that sent glittering shoots of water into the still air. Lights blazed in the portico leading to the entrance foyer but Ash drove around the back to the private entrance. Nasim came to open his door, while another red-liveried servant went around to Sally's door as soon as he'd parked. He waited for Sally to join him. "My mother has a private entrance here, so she does not have to mix with the hotel guests," he explained, low-voiced, as they followed Nasim through a doorway. Inside she hesitated, her lips an O of surprise. He supposed her reaction was to be expected. Her head swiveled, taking in the pointed arches carved in filigreed detail, decorated stone pillars, spectacular ceilings, the soft gleam of light on gold, inlaid stonework and shutters and everywhere, bright, vibrant color. Her heels clicked on the tiled floor. "It's amazing." He shrugged. "It's extravagant and overblown. But the tourists like it and they pay top dollar for the privilege." He ushered her through one more spectacular doorway where

his mother stood waiting for them. She cast a gimlet glance at Sally, then said, "Asok. So nice of you to dine with me. And this is our Australian doctor." He beckoned to Sally. "Yes. Doctor Sally Carter." His eyes met Sally's, offering encouragement. He had a feeling this wasn't going to be fun. Sally folded her hands and bowed her head. "Namaste. I'm delighted to meet you." Calculating eyes flicked over Sally's gown. He sensed disapproval, but the older woman's words were polite enough. "My son has been telling me much about you. I am hearing you are doing very well in the villages." "I'm finding my main role is to educate the women, in particular, in matters of hygiene. It's good to see that at least they have clean drinking water and that they are beginning to understand how important it is to wash their hands." His mother sank down on a low lounge. He directed Sally to another with a flick of his head and a glance, while he sat opposite her. She sat upright, tense. He wasn't really surprised. His mother could be formidable and he'd guess she'd taken a dislike to the Australian doctor, though he couldn't imagine why. He met Sally's eyes and gave her an encouraging smile, which she returned. Servants brought tea in delicate, elaborate cups. Sally sipped, listening as he talked, in English, about his visit to Europe and America, expanding his business network. Every now and then he sent her a reassuring smile so she could feel included. During a lull in the conversation he simply enjoyed her presence. "Have you traveled much, Miss Carter?" They both jumped. His mother raised an eyebrow. Sally put her cup down. "No. I was too busy learning how to be a doctor." "So you have not seen the wider world." Ash quelled his irritation. What a joke. His mother had never left India. "I'm starting now, I suppose. I've been to Bali. There's a lot of Indian culture on that island." A hint of doubt flashed across his mother's face. "Not Indian. Buddhist, I can believe." "Yes, Buddhist. But the architecture reflects what you'd find in parts of India," Ash said.

She flashed an annoyed glance at him, dismissing the notion. "There is nothing like India. It is time to eat." She summoned a hovering attendant. A servant handed Sally a thali, rice and chapatis already in place on its metal surface. No cutlery was in evidence. Ash summoned the attendant. "Spoon and forks," he murmured. "Quickly." The fellow hurried away and returned with the utensils on a tray. Ash took a fork; so did Sally, her eyes sending him a silent thank you. His mother pursed her lips. "Will you let me choose for you?" he asked Sally. She nodded, relief glowing in her eyes. "Thank you." The servant put food into the bowls on her tray at his direction, while his mother scrutinized Sally's every move with haughty disdain. "Mother, she's a guest," he murmured in Marathi. She answered in the same language. "This is India. She should try to conform." Sally scooped up one of the curries onto the rice on her fork, and ate. He'd just eaten a mouthful himself, and even he had found it hot. Sally swallowed. Her eyes bulging a little she reached for an extra piece of naan bread. Ash smiled at her and nodded, then turned to his mother. "A little hotter than your usual taste, I would have thought, Mother," he said. "Not really," she said in English. Switching to Marathi she added, "It's been such a long time since you've dined with me I'm surprised you have any idea of how spicy I like my food." He glared at her, then translated for Sally while his mother directed laser bolts at him. "I am so sorry," his mother said, a brittle smile plastered on her face. "I am not seeing my son as often as I would wish." She turned to him. "When will you be leaving again?" "Soon. I want to finalize arrangements for the call center. I'm waiting on confirmation that the finance has gone through." "Where are you building your call center?" Sally asked. He loved the sound of her voice, deeper than most women's, with that soft Australian accent, not as nasal as many he'd heard. "There's vacant land this side of Nagpur. The city fathers are keen, but I have a few more hurdles to clear." His mother curled her lip. "We have no need for that nonsense

here, Asok. You have your hotel, your tourist park. What more are you wanting?" Ash shoved his plate aside. She just wouldn't even try to understand. "There are not enough jobs for the youngsters here. The workers in the palace are from families who have always worked here and there are only so many who can work in the park. With a call center nearby, the youngsters will be encouraged to learn language and technical skills they can use and they'll be able to earn an income." "It is not part of our tradition." "Tradition doesn't feed families. They just go on and have a dozen brats they can't support..." he stopped, glaring at her. They'd had this conversation, so many times before. She thought they were all beneath her, that they didn't matter. His mother leaned toward Sally. "You see all these portraits around the walls?" "Yes," Sally, said gazing around her. "Your ancestors, I assume. I can see the family resemblance." His mother nodded. "The Bhosles are an ancient and revered line. It is going back nearly a thousand years. Portraits in the palace are going back five hundred years. How far back can you trace your family?" Sally's eyebrows shot up. "Me? Hardly at all. I met my grandparents and that's about it. I've never gone into this genealogy stuff." "So family is of no consequence to you?" His mother smiled as she said the words, but her eyes were hard. Frowning, Sally raised her head, matching his mother's stare. "That's about the size of it, yes." There was a story behind that look but now was not the time. He'd had enough. "We should go." He rose to his feet and took Sally's arm, the first time this evening he'd touched her. That thrill again, that aching longing. She looked into his eyes as she stood, her pupils so wide only a ring of blue surrounded them. "Humph." The soft sound filled the room. "You're falling for her, aren't you?" his mother said in Marathi. He let his hand drop. "She's a nice lady." "You take me for a foolish old woman? You couldn't heap enough praise on her when you told me of her talents. And now... I have eyes. I see how you look at her, how she looks at you. She is

not Indian, she cannot be anything more than a distraction for you." He sucked in a breath. He'd no idea that it was so obvious. "She's here for five more months and then she goes home." "And meanwhile she lives in your house, with you, when you are there." "Enough of this, Mother. You're talking nonsense." He turned to Sally and said in English, "I'm sorry. A private matter." He managed a smile. "Namaste, Mother." She returned the gesture. Holding Sally's arm he led her to the door, where he released his grip on her. An attendant held the car doors open for them. She slipped inside and fastened the seat belt while he started the engine and rolled the vehicle out of the car park. "Please excuse my mother," Ash said. "She is of the old aristocracy, too proud by half. I didn't expect her to be so rude." Sally glanced at him. "Did I do something wrong?" He lifted one hand from the steering wheel for a moment. Wrong. What can a woman do wrong to a mother? "She is protective of me. I am her only child." "She wants to protect you from me?" He tapped his fingers on the steering wheel. That was about the size of it. The cruiser forged through the darkness, the headlights carving a path. He parked the car and walked around to her side, where she waited, gazing at him. "My mother thought there was something between us." The look in her eyes was enough. He felt the electricity between them, a current drawing them closer. He cupped her cheek with one palm, and she nestled against his hand. Hardly aware of what he was doing he slipped an arm around her waist and pulled her against him. "Sally?" He bent his head, angling for a kiss. Even as he told himself he shouldn't do this, her hands slid up to his shoulders and her lips met his, soft and gentle, an enquiring sort of kiss. She tasted of curry and tea. She leaned into him, eyes closed, as he altered his grip, pulling her tightly to his body while his tongue probed the softness of her mouth. He was so hard it hurt, his erection a solid ridge wedged between their bodies. To hell with his mother. They were adults, weren't they? He drew away, his chest heaving. "Come." His arm around her waist, he

led her up the steps to the veranda and opened the door. Along the passage to his room... She slowed, held back and stopped outside her bedroom door. "Ash, no." He frowned, reached out for her. "What?" She put her hands on his chest, gentle but as implacable as a brick wall. "Best not to start. It will only end in tears." Her eyes glistening, she tried for a smile as she pushed him away. He stood for a moment, just looking at the closed door. The sense of loss swept through him, leaving him empty. I want you, so badly. His lips still tingled with the taste of her, the scent of her perfume lingered in his nose. She wanted him, too, no doubt about that. He sucked in a deep breath. Ah, she was probably right. If he fell in love it would be even worse when she left him and went home to Australia. Even so, the longing was a physical ache. "You will let her go?" "She is not Indian. How many times?" He walked uncomfortably the last few steps to his own room, peeling off his jacket as he went. A cold shower would have to do. For now.

Chapter 7 ​ She walked along the jungle path between the crowding, clutching branches, unease growing with every step. It was here, somewhere, she felt the panic roiling in her gut. When it landed in front of her she whirled and ran, ran from the glowing golden eyes. The beast bounded behind her, the heavy paws thumping on the ground. Thud... thud... She heard its breath hissing between its teeth. With a shaking hand Sally wiped sweat from her forehead. Again. Her heart hammered, pounding in her chest. It was so real, as if the tiger was going to catch her. She sat up and turned on the bedside lamp. Near enough to 5am. At least she didn't have to work today. And if she wasn't mistaken, Ash would be home soon. Damn it, don't think about him. Fat chance of that. She'd thought about him every day, wondered where he was, what he was doing. And it was more than a physical attraction. She loved his smile, the way he walked, almost prowled. And he was always so kind and gentle and attentive. She huffed a sigh. And unattainable. Even if he wanted her, too, even if he fell in love, it would be wrong. They were from different worlds. It would never work. She scrambled out of bed and fetched a glass of water from the kitchen, slopping only a little on the bench as she poured. A dream, just a dream. As she gulped the water down, a shadow appeared beside her. ASH STARED DOWN AT Sally. She'd almost dropped the glass, her eyes as round and frightened as a Chital caught in headlights. "Are you all right?" Ash said. She gaped at him, but the tension had drained. She even looked pleased to see him. She smiled. "Yes. A dream, that's all." She raised the glass. "I just wanted a glass of water. Sorry if I disturbed you." "I just got in." Even tousled from sleep she looked delectable, a

silky cream robe wrapped around her body. He couldn't resist following the line of the fold between her breasts. He'd bet she was naked apart from the robe. She could. Macaque males stood upright on their hindlegs, barking calls to females who gathered their young close to their chests and scrambled into the higher branches of the trees. Maybe just a male." A low rumble and a cloud of dust attracted her. Across a meadow of yellowish grass backs rose and fell, here and there an antlered head poked above the galloping herd. Chital, the smaller, spotted red deer.

"There." Mahdur pointed at a tree on the other side of the river. "A big male." She peered along his arm, acutely aware of Ash right beside her. He crept toward the unsuspecting prey, the stripes on his coat matching the pattern of light and shade in the long grass. His belly almost brushing the ground he placed each foot with care, not breaking a twig, hardly raising a murmur, not even a whisper in the wind. When a head was lifted in the herd, he froze. The head dropped and he resumed his stalk. Sally leaned further across the howdah's edge to eliminate a tree branch in the view finder and focused the camera, her finger poised on the shutter. The tiger's muscles bunched. She was there with him, watching the prey he'd selected, a big doe. The deer tore at the grass, its ears twitching at buzzing insects. Now. He moved suddenly, explosively, crashing through the undergrowth. The sambal scattered, the alarm calls rang in the trees. The doe he'd singled out swerved this way and that to avoid

the clutching claws. The heat of the chase filled Sally, intent, eyes fixed on the darting doe and then the final surging leap as fangs sank into soft tissue, blood spurted, teeth ground on bone. "I am so sorry, Raja-sahib. She is jittery, more than I have ever seen." The lens was worthless, the case crushed, the glass misplaced and scratched. Judging by the cracks in the body the internal processor wouldn't have survived, either. But maybe, if she was very lucky, the SD card would be okay. Forcing the cover open she slid the card out, mental fingers crossed. She wouldn't know until she could get it back to a computer to check the contents. "I'm so sorry, Miss." bottle and swallowed a few mouthfuls. That was better. Ash smiled. "You were lucky. The hunt is not often a success." "No?" clinic building where villagers had already gathered. As usual, they were mostly women wrapped in saris, a few with children on their hips. He ranted at her in Marathi. "Sorry, I don't understand," she said in English. Ela stood. "He said—" "I speak English. This...," he searched for a word, "this peasant can wait. He is laborer. THE FRONT PICKET FENCE outside the little house in Fitzroy needed paint but the postage stamp front yard was neat. Sally opened the gate, fumbling for the front door key. This one. changed. The main bedroom on the left, sitting room opposite. Further up, one door to her room, facing the other door to Robert's. Down the end, the kitchen, then the bathroom and laundry. this, he'd say yes. His interests overlapped hers. Damn it. If he could just get a look at the blasted parcel. How? The answer was obvious. Inside his head the tiger purred. "Sounds like fun. He killed some time around the stalls and shops until late, then walked through the street markets where the vendors were packing up for the night, tossing their refuse into the overflowing gutters. A huge black rat peered at him and scurried off. The herbalist was still open. Ash waited, merging with the shadows, a part of the darkness beside the front door, until the street had almost emptied. If he didn't move soon, the owner would lock up and leave. He allowed the tiger darkness to morph his features slightly and went in the front door. The proprietor looked up, ready to say something. Ginger, lemon, lavender, cardamom, cloves and other, less pleasant odors, all competed for his attention. He singled out the tiger scent. Polystyrene packaging lay under the workbench. The box reeked of tiger. The wrapping had been discarded, tossed into a cardboard box with other refuse. He pulled the paper out and turned it over in his hands. The address was in Chinese, but the sender was a medical laboratory in Nagpur. He growled, a deep rumble in his chest. This he could follow. He took a notebook from his pocket and wrote down the address. "Kill him," growled the tiger. "Let me tear out his throat." "Don't be stupid." But he could not do nothing. "No." He leaned against the wall and pushed the

beast back. "It will do more harm than good." He shoved the tiger parts into a bag, then sniffed around for any pills or concoctions that had even a trace of tiger scent. Most he stowed in the bag with the organs. The herbalist had begun to stir, moaning. Ash receded far enough to the other side to distort his features again. He smeared some of the tiger ointments on the herbalist's clothes. The man's nose twitched. His eyes opened, narrow slits at first until he saw what leaned over him, first shock, then horror, his mouth agape. Ash lifted his lips to show his fangs. The stink of excrement bore witness to the herbalist's terror. And to leave him a lasting warning... he opened the man's shirt, exposing a pale chest, and let his claws extend. Fighting the temptation to rend, he scored the flesh, four talons wide. Blood welled, filling his nostrils with the exciting scent of killing. The were-tiger in his mind ran his tongue over his fangs. The herbalist fainted. Ash stepped back, a deliberate, conscious effort, and shoved the tiger back. It snarled its defiance. His chest heaving, he took the bag of tiger parts from the counter and left the shop, closing the door behind him.

Chapter 24 ​ Sally walked through the village to Haji's house, carrying her folder of photos and gifts for the kids. Everyone she passed smiled and said hello, welcome back, so glad you returned. It felt good, it really did. Haji held the door wide open for her. "So good to see you back, Doctor Sally." She stepped inside into humid dimness, where Haji's wife, Sita, and the children waited, wide smiles on their faces. She returned the namastes. The old lady's chair still stood in its corner, forlorn and empty. Mothers. She couldn't say she missed hers. Sorry, Mum. "We were very sad to hear of your mother," Sita said. "It is a great loss." What could she say? What would these people understand? "Thank you. As you say, death is a new beginning." "May her next life be a better one." Sita bowed her head. And so say all of us. "I'm sure it will be." Sita called them to eat outside, under a mango tree. "In Australia in the northern parts they have weather like this. They call the heat before the rain the 'silly season' because people do stupid things. Do they call it something like that here?" Of course they did. Haji told her the word. "We pray for the monsoon, for the rain to start and bring life to the rivers and the forest." After dinner, Sally pulled out her photos. "It seems I have Indian blood." She showed them the pictures of her great-great-grandmother as a child and as a bride. "Her name was Sita." "From Rajasthan." Haji turned to her, examining her face. "You

look a little like her. Especially around the eyes." Wow. The resemblance must be quite marked. "They were married and had children and so on up through the generations. So I'm six point two-five percent Indian. How 'bout that?" Haji laughed and bowed, offering her a special namaste. "Welcome home." Home. She certainly felt a greater affinity for India than she had before. "So, what's been happening since I've been away?" Not a lot, it seemed. The mahouts reported finding a den with three new cubs, which helped to compensate for the loss of those killed by the victorious male. "Do you share that with your class?" Sally said, sipping on herbal tea. "Oh, yes. It is their heritage." "Even the deaths? The dead cubs?" He waggled his head. "The older ones know, anyway. The children of mahouts find out from their fathers." "Yes, I guess so. And they all know about the Black Tiger." He smiled. "This story intrigues you." "It does. Mahdur said in the past bodies had been found with their throats torn out. Have you heard those?" He cradled his cup in his hands. Ali and Nasim had been shooed off to bed. "I have heard them. I don't know if they are true. But there is one story I know which I do believe. I heard this from my mother, who was told by her mother. It was in the days of the British Raj. A British officer came here, with his red coat and superior airs. He told the raja he wanted to hunt tigers." "Told?" "Yes, told. This was in the days before the Rebellion against British rule in 1857. That was how it was. Of course, the raja refused. The English colonel tried to bribe the mahouts but they refused to take him and the raja supported the mahouts. In the end the officer took the raja's wives and children as hostage and insisted on a tiger hunt in exchange for their release. The raja directed one of the senior mahouts to take the officer out on his elephant. In his conceit, he went alone, armed with his rifle." Haji stopped to sip his tea. "Come on, what happened? The tiger killed him?" Haji's lips jerked in a tiny smile that quickly disappeared. "Yes. The story was that a tiger leapt at the officer on the elephant, killed

him in the howdah." "Tigers will do that? Attack an elephant?" "Not so much the elephant as the man on its back. Yes, it happens." "And this was the Black Tiger?" Haji nodded. "My mother was a direct descendant of that mahout. He swore to the raja and to his colleagues the tiger that attacked the elephant was black. It tore the man's throat out in the howdah, a handspan from where he sat on the elephant's neck. The elephant panicked of course, and charged off. The tiger leapt down with the man's body in his jaws." Savage elation tingled every nerve in her body. She reeled. She could have sworn she heard a voice in her head, just at the edge of hearing, snarl, 'murderer'. Haji leaned toward her, his hand outstretched. "Are you all right? You look as if you've seen a ghost." She swept her hand back through damp hair. "Uh, yes. Just tired I guess. Did they recover the body?" "Yes, the mahout found it on the way back to the palace, where the tiger had dropped it. The corpse was undamaged, except for the torn throat. No one pushed the issue of tiger hunting in Tengai again." "So your ancestor actually saw the Black Tiger?" "Yes. And that is the significance. It is the only time the beast has been seen by a reliable witness. The mahout said it stared into his eyes before it leapt down with its kill. He thought he would die, too. The tiger waited until the elephant was nearly past, then came down from the height, so it could attack the man in the howdah." Sally gazed past the friendly glow of light into darkness. In the silence the rustles and chirps of furtive night creatures sounded loud. In this land filled with history, the past crowded close, superstition came to life. She shivered, despite the warmth. "Couldn't it just have been an ordinary tiger, though?" Haji shrugged. "I think we modern people are too inclined to discount the recollections of the past. All they told the British was that a tiger killed the colonel. In those times, death from a tiger was a risk hunters took. But the mahout had no reason to lie to the raja." She rose to her feet. So Haji, at least, thought the tiger was real.
"No, I guess not. Loved the story. Lessons at the same time?" She waited for the nod. "Good night."

Chapter 25 ​ She was in the jungle again, that tunnel of undergrowth that led to the temple. As soon as she recognized the place her heart began to race. The tiger would be here, somewhere. But no. She felt no sense of his presence. She edged forward, creeping down the path until she stood under the last great teak tree. The blank rock wall rose beyond the clearing but in the centre something gleamed. Nothing stirred. She slunk closer and recognized a pool, reflecting moonlight. She leaned over the edge... Sally put out a hand, groping for a light while the blood pounded in her pulse. Hand, let it be a hand, not a paw. The light glowed. Her heart thundering, she flexed her fingers. She'd seen a tiger reflected in the water, staring up at her. But it wasn't him, not that big male. This was a female, as midnight-black as he was, where her face should have been. God, she'd let this place get to her. She'd only been back for a week and she was freaking out. Her great-great-grandmother had died insane. Maybe the same thing was happening to her. Ash. The notes of Beethoven's 'Für Elise' rang out soft and clear. Her cell phone. She picked it up from the bedside table, where the bedside clock registered 2:33. "Doctor Carter," she said. His voice sounded tinny in the speakers.

"I'm going nuts here." She swallowed. "Dreams again. Nightmares." Just like her great-great-grandmother who ended up in an asylum. "Sally... calm down. Are you on Skype?" "Yes." "Go and start your computer. I'm 'ashindia456'. Call me. I want to see you." Oh, shit. See her in 2:30am glory, bleary eyed and tousled? "Ash, I—" "Do it. Now. Please." She stopped off at the bathroom to run a comb through her hair before she fired up the laptop. The photo of the tigress and her three cubs filled the screen as she typed his ID into the Skype interface. Ash's image appeared as soon as he'd accepted the call. He looked disheveled, his chest bare. "You're all right?" he asked immediately. "What's happening to you there, now?" "Now?" "Now. Something happened. What?" "A nightmare, that's all. Just a nightmare." She scrubbed her hands back through her hair. Another fucking nightmare. And just now was the worst. It was so real. "Ever since I went to the temple they've been getting worse." When she opened her eyes he was staring at her, a sparkle in his eyes. He straightened, beaming. "It's all right, love. It's all right. I'll come home. Don't go near the temple. Understand?" She nodded. He seemed happy but he was warning her. "Okay. But Ash, what is it? Is it dangerous?" "Dangerous, oh, yes. But not, I think, to you." He leaned forward. "Remember, I told you there were things to explain? Things to do with the temple?" He waited until she'd nodded. "Just stay away and I'll explain when I see you. Promise me?"

A half-smile hovered around his mouth. Was that supposed to make her feel better? Because it didn't. "Ash—" He held up a hand. "Promise? I'll catch a plane later today. I should be home this afternoon or evening and then I'll explain everything." Some of the fear faded. He was coming to explain. Maybe she wasn't going mad. "I promise. Thanks. Thanks so much." WHEN SHE RETURNED FROM surgery at the end of her working day, Sally bent over the computer, set up as usual on the dining room table, and checked the treatment stats Ela had entered into a spreadsheet for her. clouds, was heading for the horizon. He'd said this evening. Where was he? At the sound of 'für Elise' she darted inside and snatched the phone from the table. "Ash?" I'm about at the end of my tether, Ash. I haven't slept properly since I got back from Melbourne." "I'll be back tomorrow. I promise. Love you." "I love you, too, Ash." He was gone. She blinked away tears.

Chapter 26 ​ Sally emerged from her room at three minutes to eight. At least she'd managed to sleep without dreaming, but she still felt like she'd been shoved through a wringer. She swung into her robe and went off to the kitchen to make a cup of tea. She was sitting at the bench with her cup when her phone beeped. An SMS from Ash. He'd be back mid-afternoon if all went according to plan. Damn. Now she had a morning to kill. Too late to hitch a ride with one of the tour parties leaving the palace in a land cruiser to hunt for tigers. Then again, the prospect of having to share a tour guide with a bunch of Germans and Americans didn't appeal at all. A visit to the palace, perhaps? She'd been there many times to see the rani, but she'd never seen the rest of the place. She could do the palace tour, have a look at this mausoleum he'd been brought up in. She'd been meaning to do it for ages, but every time something had intervened. She could kill a couple of hours and be back at the park waiting for him. She drove up to the hotel just before eleven, when the next tour started, and went up to the counter in the souvenir shop to buy a ticket, two hundred rupees, a little over four Australian dollars. "Okay to take photos?" The young man beamed. "Yes, madam. Certainly. If you will wait in the foyer the guide will come soon." She took the time to admire the entrance hall, with its mosaic floor and decorated marble pillars supporting a vaulted ceiling. A couple of tourists descended the marble staircase, the American accents bouncing off the walls. "Is this where the tour starts? Good. I'm looking forward to seeing the women's quarters." Sally hung back in the corner, inspecting the camera. Lens clean, battery full, SD card empty. The sound of lowered voices attracted her. Mister Kumar stood in earnest conversation with one of the staff, a young man of Chinese appearance. Well, why wouldn't he?

He managed the estate and presumably the staff. Yet this conversation seemed furtive, their heads too close together for a normal staff-management exchange. Odd. Another tourist wandered down the central staircase, the young man Kumar had been talking to hurried off and Kumar turned, catching sight of her. "Oh. Doctor Sally." Had she imagined that look of consternation before he stepped forward with his usual smile? "Are you here to see the rani?" he said. "You don't usually use this entrance?" She brandished the camera. "No, I'm going to do the palace tour." He gazed at her over the top of his glasses, eyes full of reproach. "But you had only to ask. I would have escorted you myself." "Well, if you have time." He shook his head. "Not today. I am about to leave for a family celebration. Tomorrow?" "Thanks, but I've a few hours to myself now. I'll do the tour." "The tour doesn't show everything." "If there's anything else I'd like to see, or I should see, maybe you can show me another day." He shrugged. "As you wish. It would be my pleasure." He frowned, gazing down at the stub in her hand. "But you have bought a ticket." "It's fine. Honestly." He insisted on refunding the admission fee, then disappeared into the bowels of the palace with a smile and a wave. The tour started promptly at eleven. Their guide introduced himself and led them through room after room overflowing with ostentatious wealth. Sally took pictures of vases and urns, filigreed gold, wall murals of tigers, leopards, sambal and the rare Indian wolves. "Are they the wolves from Kipling's Jungle Book?" someone asked, pointing at the painting. "They are, madam. But they are very rare now. As rare as the tigers." "You got any heads?" an American asked. He had his hands thrust in his pockets. "Heads, sir?" The tourist shifted his chewing gum to his other cheek. "You

know. Tiger heads. Yeah, or skins. Rugs. Hunt trophies." "There were some trophies in past times. But they were in poor condition and the present raja had them destroyed." Yes, she'd bet he did. "No. You pay now. Much danger for me."

"Half now. Half later when you bring tiger." "Forty thousand. Now." "Too much. Twenty." "No. Thirty." "Is a lot." "Is big danger for me. And I can bring tiger today, tonight." "Today?" The Indian passed her not a few feet away, young, dressed in the uniform of a park forest worker. Footsteps—hopefully the Asian's—crunched through the gravel heading in the opposite direction. Thirty thousand rupees for the life of a tiger. Oh, sure, it was a fortune for him but it was a little more than six hundred Australian dollars, probably a few nights' tariff in this hotel. Ash had said they could make fifty thousand US from one carcass. Obscene. She slipped out of the bush. The Asian had retreated toward the palace. He wore a palace uniform. The man she'd seen Kumar talking to? It didn't matter. She hurried as quickly as she dared after the Indian, her camera in her hands as if looking for photo opportunities. He stood next to a truck, one of the vehicles they used for forest maintenance, talking to another man and the body language was furtive. Heads together, glances around, they'd both be in it, no question. Sally strolled to her own vehicle, parked in the hotel's parking area. What to do? Tell somebody here? But who? The staff and the tourists had disappeared, sheltering from the oppressive heat. Besides, how many of them would be involved? She didn't know any of these men and twenty thousand rupees was a lot of money in this country. Ash's mother? She dismissed the notion as soon as it formed. Kumar? She tried his cell phone. No signal, not even enough to leave a message. Oh, yes. He'd gone somewhere for a family celebration. Jay? The call rang out. He and the other rangers used radios in

the park, not cell phones. She placed her camera equipment on the passenger seat next to her and kept an eye on the poachers. She could ring Ash, at least ask for advice. She pressed the speed dial. Please, please answer. The answering service kicked in straight away. 'Hello, you've reached Ash. Leave a message and I'll call back.' This was his private cell phone. It must have been turned off. She hung about for as long as she dared, then sighing in exasperation, she started up the cruiser and headed out along the curved driveway and onto the road. Ah. A piece of luck. The heat beat down on the cruiser's roof, forcing the air conditioner to work hard. She should have seen the truck's dust by now. The sign for the turn-off to the village appeared. Bugger. They must have left the road. She slammed the car into reverse, turned around and headed back the way she'd come, searching the right side of the road. Tire tracks led into a narrow trail. windscreen. The track ended at the river, she'd guess not too far from where she'd been those many weeks ago with Ash. thought that far. The truck's window went down. They'd long since turned the engine off. A narrow cylinder that had to be a rifle barrel protruded from the driver's side. Then he stripped off his sweat-soaked shirt, shoes, pants and put them in the backseat. He stepped back. Now.

The tiger growled. Ash felt his body stretch, expand, his center of gravity descend as he dropped to all fours, the fangs fill his mouth, his ankles rise, his tail swish behind him.
