The manager's lip curled. "I don't trust you. Not for a moment. You'd kill anybody for your precious tigers. Well, I've got two hostages now. Helicopter. Money. Mess me around and I'll send your mother down the stairs and I'll still have the Australian doctor you lust after." "She says one leap and I can take him down," Sally said. "Yes, but can you control her?" "We have to do something." "Don't let her kill!" "I'm coming up, Kumar," Ash said. Kumar aimed the gun at him, holding the weapon in both hands. "I'll shoot." "If you shoot me, that's murder." Ash put a foot on the lowest step. "Murder is a capital offence." Another step.

Sally leapt without warning, blackness swirling around her. She hit Kumar in the shoulder. The gun fired but Kumar twisted around, wrestling with her, kicking out at the wheelchair, which teetered. Ash bounded up the stairs, covering the stairs in two leaps. He shoved the wheel chair out of the way. Sally had changed. Her shirt hung in tatters from massive black shoulders. Kumar lay on his back, his eyes round with shock as he shoved at the animal's neck. She snarled, her jaws reaching down for Kumar's throat. "Change! Change back now. Order her," he said to his alter ego. "Do it." She backed off but her paws still rested on the man's chest. "She wants to kill," the human Sally whimpered while the tiger snarled, the long canines glinting. Ash grabbed the loose skin at her neck. "Change!" The tiger dissolved into mist and Sally appeared, her clothes hanging off her in tatters. "I'm sorry," she said, collapsing into his arms. "Asok, the gun," the rani shouted, pointing. Kumar had struggled to his knees and was reaching for the discarded weapon. Ash whirled and kicked the pistol, sending it clattering along the tiles. Kumar backed off, his eyes bright with fear and madness. He pointed a trembling finger over Ash's shoulder at Sally. "Her. She's a monster. Don't come near me, don't touch me." Ash raised a hand but Kumar had scrambled onto the balustrade. So he thought she was the monster, did he? Little did he know. Inside his mind the tiger swished his tail, head lowered for the charge. "Behave yourself." "Kumar, come down. Let's talk." Kumar edged further back, scrabbling for a handhold. His grip gave way. His despairing cry echoed as he plunged backwards. The crack as his head struck the tiled floor ten meters below was followed by the thud of the body settling. The tiger growled. Sally was already running, leaping down the stairs to where the manager lay spread-eagled on his back, blood pooling around his head. Feeling for a pulse, she said, "Call an ambulance." Ash did as she asked. "Is he alive?" "Barely. I doubt if he'll make it. I'd say he has a cracked skull." She sank back on her haunches. The door edged open and a face peered around. "Raja-sahib?" Damn. And Sally like that.

"Asok, what is happening?" The rani called from the top of the stairs, her voice querulous, anxious. "Sally, take my mother to her quarters and find some clothes. I'll deal with the staff." Sally raced up the staircase. He waited til she'd pushed the wheelchair out of sight before he called the staff in.

Chapter 33 ​ Fragments of clothing littered the floor at the top the steps. The rest flapped around Sally's body, leaving not much to the imagination. Something silver caught her attention. Sally picked up the chain and let the necklace dangle from her hand. Should she put it on, around her neck? "You don't need it anymore," the tigress purred. "I am with you now." "You're going to have to learn to behave yourself. I nearly killed that man." "He is a murderer. And I am a tiger." "Sally?" The rani was staring at her. Sally tried a smile. "Sorry. A lot of things have happened in a very short time." She handed the necklace to the rani. "Hold this for me, will you?" She took the handles of the chair while the rani gazed at the crystal in the palm of her hand. "So. How can you be a were-tiger? Is it this?" "You've seen it before, I expect. Ash gave it to me in the temple." She twisted around in the chair. "The tiger temple? You have been in there?" "Yes." Sally maneuvered the chair through the door and into the bedroom. "Look, maybe we'd better wait for Ash." The rani fell silent, staring at something Sally couldn't see. "Clothes?" Sally said. "Of course." The rani waved her hand. "In the wardrobe. Wear a sari. I'll show you how." The older woman eased herself out of the chair. "I'm fine to walk—just not the stairs." "No pain?" Sally asked. "A little. But the hip grows stronger every day." She limped into the walk-in robe and ran a critical glance along the row of

garments. "This one." She pulled out a blue sari and a cream bodice while Sally shrugged off what was left of her clothes. The rani showed her how to wind the silken material around her waist and then up over her shoulder. Sally admired herself in the full-length mirror. "Looks good," she said, smiling. And it did. The material complemented her slim figure, flowing around her hips, and the color set off her dark blue eyes. The rani nodded and led Sally back to her sitting room. "Now we wait for my son," she said, sinking into a chair. A servant appeared, her face flushed. She asked a question in which Sally recognized 'well' and 'would you like tea'? "I would like tea," Sally said in her best Marathi. The rani smiled the widest smile Sally had seen on her face and sent the girl off. "You have learnt." "My father taught me to try." "And your mother?" Sally waved a hand. "May she rest in peace." I don't want to go there. The older woman nodded. "Do you have siblings? A brother or sister?" "A brother. We're not close." "It is strange, this. For an Indian. You don't care about family. For us, it is everything." Ash appeared in the doorway. He halted, a grin spreading over his face. "A sari. It suits you." He covered the few steps to the sofa and sat beside Sally. "He's been taken to hospital. They think brain damage." "Not much doubt about that," Sally said. "What about the police?" He shook his head. "It was an accident, not a police matter. But I will need a new estate manager. For now, I'll have to do it myself." He leaned toward his mother. "You weren't hurt, Mother?" "No. Frightened, but not hurt. And when the doctor became a tiger... it was a shock. An astonishment. How is this possible?" "She has Indian blood. Indians went to Australia and a—how many greats, Sally?" "Great-great-grandmother," Sally said. "Yes. She was Indian. I think from Rajasthan. We can trace our family back to Rajasthan, albeit not legitimate," Ash finished. A slight frown creased the rani's brow. "What sort of family?"

Ash took Sally's hand. "Her ancestor's father was a cameleer." Frowning, the rani pursed her lips. Oh, dear. Not good enough for her. Before she could say anything, Ash said, "Our family started off as warlords, Mother. Brigands. You think that's better? Besides, she is the one." He lifted Sally's hand. "I've dreamed of tigers all my life," Sally said. "Now, I think I understand. This other side of me was trying to connect with me through dreams." The crystal lay on the table between them, the broken chain snaking across the inlaid surface. "That was the break- through. I put it on and the connection was made. I don't need it anymore." The rani picked up the crystal claw. "I can feel how it might call to you, I sense the blackness, but that is all. You say it was in the temple?" She turned to her son. "And you took her there?" "I did." He stared at the floor for a moment. "I killed a man. I changed to the tiger to save Sally from death at the hands of a poacher. She had risked her life to frighten off a tiger who would have been shot. "I've been thinking for some time that Sally was more than just a foreign doctor. We could sense each other. I knew when she dreamt of the black tiger, she knew when I was in danger. So, after she knew what I was, I took her to the temple." "Perhaps for all these years we had women who could have been tigers, too," the rani said. "The world has changed." Sadness flitted across her features. "In times past a man like Kumar would not have dared to lay a hand on me or on a tiger. How has this happened?" "Greed. What else, I don't know. My guess is he dealt with the Chinese, arranging to provide them with tigers. He would know which of the locals to approach, men who knew the park and needed the money." She sighed. "I do not believe he would have hurt me, Asok. Mister Kumar was always very good to me. Even when I was," she licked her lips, "difficult." "Possibly. It might have been a bluff but I suppose we'll never know. I'll get my accountants in to check the books," Ash said. "I know he liked to gamble." "So you will marry?" The rani swiveled her head, looking from Sally to Ash and back. Sally felt the flush burning up her neck. In her mind the tigress

lifted her head. Ash squeezed her hand. "I have asked her." The rani raised her eyebrows. "What is there to ask? She must marry you." Anger seared up Sally's spine. "Of course you'll marry him," said her alter ego. "You've waited far too long already." Sally sighed. "I really don't need you running my life, you know," she replied. The rani tutted, dark brows drawn together. "I would have preferred an Indian girl, of course. But... it is less important than the tiger heritage and you clearly have that. So. Welcome. I look forward to grand children." Ash was grinning, a twinkle in his dark eyes. If she looked closely she could almost see the tiger too, just beyond the wall of reality. "Well, Sally?" "I don't think I ever really had a choice. But that's fine with me." She flung an arm around his neck and kissed him. In her mind the were-tiger rumbled her approval.

From the author THANKS FOR READING Black Tiger. I hope you enjoyed the story. I've had a love affair with India for a long time, ever since university where I studied Indian history as part of my BA (Hons). I've tried my best to portray a contemporary Indian setting in what is a fantasy novel. If my Indian readers note any mistakes, I ask their forgiveness and their indulgence, because I've written this book for the tigers. I've always been an animal lover and like many other people, I adore the big cats, especially that magnificent solitary hunter, the tiger. I was horrified to learn that there are no more than two and a half thousand tigers still in the wild. Their numbers dwindle every year, through poaching and habitat destruction. In such a crowded country as India, the vast tracts of land needed for a viable wild tiger population can be difficult to justify. To its credit, the Indian Government has set aside large areas and removed villages in places like Pench to provide habitat. The development of tiger parks for tourists wishing to see the tigers in the wild is a viable way of conserving the tigers, as well as providing employment for the people. It's worked here in Australia, where humpback whales have recovered from the brink of extinction and people flock to see them in the waters near where I live. The alternative is to see them in zoos. Did you know there are more Bengal tigers in the US than there are in the wild? They're in legitimate zoos, private zoos and private hands. As a result, there is a Big Cat Rescue organization in Florida which provides a sanctuary for 'unwanted, abused or abandoned big cats.' In 2011, the owner of a private zoo released all his animals, then shot himself. The police were forced to shoot many of the roaming animals, including eighteen Bengal tigers. Tigers are not pets; they don't belong in zoos – even if we must have some in controlled environments to ensure their survival.

Poaching is a disgusting business. Tradition dies hard, but it's pretty hard to justify the use of tiger body parts in traditional medicine. Ingesting bits of tiger doesn't make you a tiger. The prognosis is not good. Without support and action, tigers will be extinct in the wild in decades, if not less. You know William Blake's immortal poem? Tyger, tiger, burning bright in the forests of the night It will be a sad day indeed if that bright light is extinguished forever.

White Tiger NEW YORK IS NO PLACE for a tiger – not for weretiger Sally Carter or for the white tiger she finds in a Harlem basement, guarding an enormous stash of heroin. Sally’s daring rescue of the tiger attracts journalist Dave Gardner, who sniffs a story and a lead to a drug baron he’s being trying to nail for years. While Sally is determined that the white tiger will find a home in a sanctuary, Gardner follows a tenuous trail from the tiger back to the drug cache – and a whole lot of trouble. Soon Sally and her weretiger husband find themselves mixed up in a drug baron’s plot for revenge where even their amazing weretiger talents may not be enough to save Gardner – or themselves. Dedication This book is dedicated to all the wonderful people in wild animal sanctuaries across the United States of America who work hard to save big cats and other beasts from a miserable life in inadequate housing. Tiger Territory is not a real place. It's an amalgam of a number of different cat sanctuaries in the US, mixed liberally with some imagination.

Chapter 1 ​ Sally eased her way between two yellow cabs blocking the intersection and scampered across the road with the rest of the New York commuters. Who worried about red lights? You took your chance when it came. She stepped aside to avoid a woman pushing a pram and found herself face to face with yet another tee-shirt vendor's cart. A row of white shirts emblazoned with 'I ♥ NY' hung along a rail. Her lips lifting in a sneer, she strolled on. Yes, she could imagine a lot of people did love the Big Apple but she wasn't one of them. Too much traffic, too many people, too many buildings crowding in close, leaning over her. She could taste the air, car exhausts, cooking odors from the roadside vendors' carts, the stink of an unwashed body, perfume, cologne. That was one of the downsides of cohabiting your mind and body with a weretiger. Her sense of smell was heightened, even when she didn't deliberately employ the cat's sensitive nose. "I don't like it here," the weretiger grumbled in her mind. "Too bad. Ash has to do business, so we're stuck." Sally wondered how his negotiations were going. It was hard to imagine her husband would like this city any more than she did. She maneuvered around the scaffolding set over the sidewalk, sidling sideways to allow a vastly overweight man to pass her. "Can we go to that open place? Where they had the trees and the lake?" the weretiger pleaded. Central Park. Yes, it was her favorite part of New York, too. "Aysha, we've been there three times already." "There is grass. And animals." Aysha licked her lips. So did Sally. Sally felt that tingle of predator that Ash had explained came with the territory. She had learned to avoid zoos, including the one in Central Park, but it was impossible to avoid the carriage horses. "I don't think they'd be too impressed with you bringing down one of the horses, my dear. But okay, we'll go to Central Park." If the weather

stayed reasonable. Clouds had thickened over the city and a cold breeze probed at her light jacket. The rain fell as Sally waited at an intersection, not heavy, but persistent. Damn. She searched for a patch of blue somewhere. Anywhere. But the cloud cover was uniform. What now? Sally gazed around her. She didn't fancy wandering under dripping trees. Maybe she could kill some time in the Natural History Museum? If the weather fined up, she could go to the park later. Scampering with her collar turned up, Sally ran for the nearest subway entrance. "Huh. So where do we go now?" "A museum." Ignoring the cat's exasperated huff, Sally clattered down the stairs into the subway, found the right line and bought a day ticket. The platform was crowded. Of course. But at least the trains came often. Soon enough the wind that preceded an oncoming train ruffled her hair. Aiming for a not too overcrowded carriage, she surged forward with everybody else and managed to snare a seat beside a large black woman. Twice the train stopped, people poured out, more people flowed in, almost like a tide. Groups gathered around the doors. Hands grasped the backs of seats. She glanced up at the line map. Next station, West 81st,, under the Natural History Museum. Some garbled announcement floated through the station, then the doors soughed shut and the train shot forward. Faster and faster. Sally straightened up. Shit. What was happening? Unconcerned passengers swayed with the carriage's motion. The big black woman next to her grinned. "Dis an express, honey. Next stop, Harlem." "Harlem?" Sally gulped. She'd heard about Harlem. Black street gangs, violence, rotting houses. "I suppose I can get a train back." "Sure. Just cross over to d'udder line. No problem." The woman settled back into her seat, her bag clutched tightly in her lap. The train slowed. People rose from seats, edged closer to the doors, like greyhounds at a starting gate. The big woman beside Sally stirred, making it clear she wanted to stand. Sally obliged, shifting into the line of strap-hangers and leaning forward with the rest as the train rolled to a halt. Rustling, shuffling movement accompanied the press to the platform. Sally got out of the way of hurrying commuters who knew what

they were doing. It was amazing how they seemed to disappear, like ants boiling out of a kicked nest. The second platform was reached via an overhead walkway. Up the stairs, over the bridge and down. She'd clearly not been the only one who'd made the mistake of catching an express. She was sure she'd seen the fellow in the business suit just crossing the walkway now, on the train. He rattled down the stairs to the other platform, where he stopped to check the board for the schedules. She'd never been to Harlem. This was a different side to New York, away from Broadway, Fifth Avenue and Times Square, beyond the high rises of the business district. And it wasn't as though she had any fear of being mugged. The worst part would be not to hurt anybody. She flexed her fingers and let a little part of the weretiger press. Talons. Aysha brightened. "We hunt?" "No, just checking we can fight back if we have to," Sally said, following the exit signs out to the street. Aysha snorted. Her backpack slung off one shoulder, Sally stepped into a street lined with New York's famous brownstones, the metal emergency exit stairs criss-crossing their facades. The rain clouds still hung low and threatening, but here, at least, the rain had stopped. Water dripped from the trees, trailed down the gutters and gathered in pools. Harlem didn't look like such a bad place. Much better than Mumbai or Kolkata. Sure, the paint was peeling here and there, but late model cars lined both sides of the street. Instead of beggars or urchins, a young black woman in denims and trainers almost jogged behind a Labrador on a leash. A few youths smoking cigarettes slouched outside a convenience store near the station's entrance. Harlem was being gentrified, she'd guess. Like her mother's little house in working class Melbourne. No garage, tiny rooms, but very close to the city centre, a Mecca for young, single people wanting the urban lifestyle. She strolled along, taking in the apartment blocks, half a dozen stories high. A car rolled down the street, the doof doof of rap music loud, despite the vehicle's closed windows. Give it a few years and those kids would be complaining of tinnitus. Sally brushed a raindrop from her cheek. Time to get back to the station and catch a nice, dry train. She crossed the road. Aysha growled. "Wait." Sally stopped. "What?" "I smell tiger."

"Don't be silly. This is a city. The world's citiest city." "I smell tiger." Sally felt her lips curl. In her own dimension, Aysha was doing the same thing, curling back her lips, her fangs exposed, her nose snuffling the air. Cautiously, Sally opened her senses to the great cat. She wasn't all that good at control, yet. If Aysha wanted to take charge... Her muscles tingled. It was so damned addictive. She and Ash had run through the jungle together several times. There was nothing like the adrenalin of being a powerful animal with a thirty foot stride, seeing through her cat's eyes, smelling a kaleidoscope of scents. She still marveled at how she could not only know what the smell meant, but also know when it was made. Almost like a time machine. "Yes. Tiger. Not far." Aysha was decisive. And she was right. Sally's heart thudded in her chest. She smelled it, too. A mix of the seductive odor of male tiger and the urine the cat had used to mark its territory. A full-grown male. Sally turned on the spot to find the source, seeking the strongest scent, while the rain came down harder, drizzling down her neck and under her clothes, a cold trickle on too-warm skin. There. Over the road. In an ordinary apartment block? Surely not. A tiger? "There," Aysha rumbled. Sally crossed over and went up the steps into a gloomy foyer. At least it wasn't raining in here, but that was about the only positive. Peeling, water-stained wallpaper hung on the walls, and the wooden floor was scuffed and dirty. The place had an elevator, the buttons scratched form years of use. She wondered if it worked. The smell of tiger was stronger. Somewhere here. There was a door in the corner, probably the stairs. The knob turned and she pushed the door open to reveal a dark, dusty stairwell, flights leading up and down. The smell of tiger rose from below, rank and dangerous. Sally's heart hammered. "He is old," Aysha murmured. "Old and hurting." Sally's fear drowned in a rising tide of fury. What sort of animal left a tiger in a basement? "Let's go see," she said to Aysha. Allowing the weretiger's senses to augment her own, Sally crept down the stairs. Somebody had been down here not too long ago. The dust on the treads was confined to the edges. That meant people came down here. The cat down there in the darkness might

not bother her, but men with guns would. Everybody in this country seemed to have a gun. She ended up on a floor covered with garbage, in front of a solid looking door. The tiger knew she was there, she heard its chuff. Sally rattled the knob. Locked, of course. She would have to break in, and she could only do that through Aysha. "Will this tiger understand you?" "Of course. It is a tiger. I have told it we will help." That was good to know. Ash had told her the tigers sensed that the weretigers were not a threat to them. But that was in India. Still, if Aysha was sure. She'd have to be careful. She couldn't afford to let the weretiger take over. Sally concentrated, letting some more of Aysha's strength seep through the barrier. Two steps back, a few deep breaths, then she kicked the door, aiming at the edge just below the lock. The door flew open, the sound of the blow echoing through the stairwell, booming and banging into eventual silence. Sally's heart beat a little faster. She hadn't counted on all that noise. She slipped into the basement, closing the ruined door behind her as best she could. The tiger stood facing her, a full grown male, one of the rare white tigers, with a collar around his neck. A cage like the ones they used for circuses was pushed up against the wall, the gate open. The stink of urine and feces almost shut her human senses down. Sally felt her clothes tighten. Aysha was asserting herself. Too much. "Not here, Aysha. Not in a city. We can't be revealed." "Huh. There is no-one to see." "Yes, but there is up there." Aysha chuffed at the tiger, which stepped forward cautiously, its head lowered. Sally put out a hand and stroked the cat's huge head. Oh, you poor, poor beast. How many years have you been down here in this prison? She scratched her fingers through his fur, fondled his ears while he pushed against her. Would it have a run? Some garden? This was wrong. Slow anger seeped up her spine. She couldn't afford to get angry. Anger led to Aysha, a full grown tiger, black as night and filled with vengeance. This might be a concrete jungle, but the Black Tiger's role was to protect its own. Control. She had to keep control. Even now she felt the tightness of her shirt as her muscles tried to change. Stupid. Stupid. She couldn't do the weretiger thing here, in broad daylight. "Settle down, Aysha. We'll find a way. But we won't achieve anything by letting you

run wild." The weretiger's growls subsided. What else was here? She gazed around the basement with her enhanced tiger vision. A metal enclosure stacked with boxes was attached to the wall opposite the tiger's cage. This must be what it was protecting. She sniffed. Heroin. Drug-dealing human parasites. Anger welled up again, and with it the siren song of the were-tiger. No. Not here. "Someone is coming," Aysha warned. Yes, damn it. She heard the rhythmic bang of footsteps on the stairs. The tiger raised his head and she sensed his anger and his fear. He growled, deep in his throat. There was nowhere to hide but she had an advantage in the dark. She flexed her hand, allowing her talons to protrude just enough. Then she jumped up and crushed the light bulb. Breathing deeply to calm herself and Aysha, she eased her way behind the heroin cage and froze. "Shaddap, you bastard." The footsteps had reached the bottom of the stairwell. Light flared through the broken door. Sally heard the man gasp, "Fuck", and then a rustle and a click. She could almost see him pull out a gun and flick off the safety.

Chapter 2 ​ Snarling, the white tiger charged the damaged door. The snarl changed to an anguished howl of pain. The tiger backed off, shaking its head. "Get back, fuck you. Get back." The voice was guttural and coarse. He pointed a black object in his hand at the tiger and pressed with his thumb. The tiger howled and slunk into the cage. Aysha took over, leaving the human Sally outside reality, watching the weretiger. It was all she could do to yell, "Don't kill!" The weretiger leapt, striking the man on the chest. "No, no... aaah." The gun went off, booming and ricocheting around the confined space. The man's body slammed onto the concrete floor. He still waved the gun in one hand. Pinning his chest with one paw, Aysha flicked the hand gun away with the other paw. Terrified eyes stared into her face. He'd emptied himself, the fouler smell of human excrement joining the rest of the fetid stench. Snarling, she grazed his neck with her teeth. He went limp. "I'm human, I'm human, I'm human," Sally muttered. And then she was, kneeling over the body of a man, her clothes tattered rags hanging over her body. Panting, she pressed her fingers to his carotid artery, which pulsed far too fast. Blood oozed from two scratches on his neck. He was lucky he'd fainted. Sally didn't think she would have been able to stop Aysha tearing his throat out, otherwise. "No," Aysha said. "He deserves no better." A deep growl reverberated. The white tiger stood beside her, his gaze fixed on his jailer. What she'd started he would finish? She pressed a hand on his shoulder, and spoke through Aysha. "No. My prey. I will finish it." His head lowered and the muscles relaxed. Sally scrambled to her feet. Somebody must have been alerted, what with the roaring and the gunshot. She wouldn't have much

time. Clothes. She needed clothes. She fumbled for the backpack, which contained a 'just in case' change for just such an emergency, light weight trousers and loose tee-shirt. Her walking shoes were undamaged. She flung off the remains of her jacket and shirt, then pulled on her garments. Just as well Ash had insisted, even when she pooh-poohed the need. Next the tiger. She tugged at the fastening for the collar, calling on a little of Aysha's strength to open clips that had rusted on. Her fingers slipped gently over the sores and her eyes filled with tears. You poor, poor beast. I'll make sure you live out your days somewhere nice. She dragged the thug into the circus cage and dropped the door, which clanged with the finality of a prison cell. She hoped. Ash's voice spoke in her mind. His calm, deep voice left her trembling. "Sally? What's happening?" She might have known he'd realize something was amiss. "Ash, I've just found a tiger in a basement in Harlem. We have to rescue him." "Calm down, Sally." Furtive footfalls sounded from the stairwell and a voice called, "Hello?" "I'm okay. But call the police, will you?" Sally called. "Ma'am-" "Don't come down here. There's a tiger." As if to underline the statement the white tiger growled softly. "Holy shit." The footsteps retreated. "Okay, I'll call the police." "Where are you, Sally?" Ash said as the sound of running feet faded up the stairs. Sally gave him the address. "Bring a transporter for the tiger. He's going to a good home." A pause. If Ash thought she was going to let them euthanize the tiger he'd better think again. " This... this bastard of a thug... he was torturing the tiger. They put a collar on him that could run an electric current through him. And... and they kept him in a frigging circus cage." The anger roared up her spine again. "He's old. And he's had a shit of a life and it isn't fair. There's got be somewhere he can go. They have zoos and things, don't they?" "All right. I'll come." Sally gathered up the fragments of her clothes and stuffed them into the backpack. Then she sat down with her back against the wall, the white tiger beside her. It did her heart good, digging her fingers into soft tiger fur. She lifted her head when sounds echoed

from above. At the same time the cage creaked. "Wha... wha happened?" Fingering his throat, the thug sat up. Sally watched the expressions pass over his face as he felt around with his hands and realized where he was. "Holy shit. Is there anyone..." He couldn't see, of course. Sally smiled to herself when the white tiger growled, that deep growl that pours into a man's mind, grasps hold of primordial fear and drags it out of the darkness. He let out a strangled gasp and struggled into the farthest corner of the cage, the metal pail clattering and banging when he pushed against it, spilling water across the floor. "Better stay in there till the police arrive, buddy. I don't think this tiger likes you very much." The cat had risen to his feet. Sally/Aysha rebuked him. "My prey." He settled, but sat with is head raised, his gaze on the door. "Ma'am? Police. Are you okay?" The voice sounded competent, if cautious. "Hi, officer," she said. "My name is Sally Carter. I'm fine. There's a stash of boxes down here which was being guarded by a tiger. The tiger is loose, so I'd suggest you stay where you are." "Can we get a clear shot at it?" "Absolutely not." Damn it, Aysha. I don't want to roar at the man. "The tiger is old and sick. You don't need to kill him." "My ass. That fuckin' animal is dangerous. It attacked me. Get me outta here!" The thug's panic-stricken voice filled the room. The white tiger snarled. "Who's that?" the policeman snapped. "Louis Romero," the thug called. "I'm the caretaker here. I don't know nothin' about heroin and no tiger. The fucker attacked me. I got scars on my neck." "Oh, listen to him," Sally groaned. "Officer, my husband, Raja Asoka Bhosle, is on his way down here. He's an Indian expert with tigers." Wasn't he just. "I've asked him to bring a transport for the tiger. We'll get the cat out of here and you can get Mister Romero to explain to you how he didn't know about the tiger, despite the electrified collar he used to control it. And by the way, Mister Romero is quite safe. I locked him in the tiger's cage." "I'm bleeding," Romero squealed. "Officer, I'm a medical doctor. Mister Romero isn't going to die of anything, except maybe his own smell, anytime soon."

The officer chuckled. "We know Mister Romero. Don't we Louis? Can I call your husband, ma'am? To confirm?" "Sure." She gave him Ash's cell phone number. Someone else had come down the stairs. The cop whispered instructions, which amounted to checking on Ash and leaving the situation as it was for the time being. "You're sure you're safe with a tiger, ma'am?" the policeman said. "It could turn on you anytime. I've heard tell you can't tame them." "No, you can't. But he's quiet enough at the moment. Best not to upset him, eh? I'm sure Ash won't be long." "Okay, ma'am. But I have a team with tranquilizer guns standing by if needed." "Sedatives can be dangerous, officer." Sally kept her hand on the tiger. He'd settled, resting his head on her thigh. She wished Ash would hurry. She'd become accustomed to the stink down here, but she could use the toilet herself, and a cup of tea would be wonderful. The tiger knew Ash had arrived before she did, sitting up on its haunches, its teeth bared to taste the air. It harrumphed softly. "Asok comes," Aysha said. Ash had never named his weretiger. Aysha had told Sally her own name, and always referred to Ash's soul mate by his true, Indian name, Asoka. Sally reached out to the white tiger. The beast was wary, recognizing the exalted status of this new visitor. "It stinks down here," Ash said, wrinkling his nose. He approached slowly, but the tiger had risen to meet him, chuffing. Ash chuffed a reply. "Hey, buddy, get me outta here," Romero pleaded. "It's dark as the pits and it stinks." The white tiger snarled at him. "Keep that thing away from me," Romero finished. He sat in the cage, as far away from the tiger as he could get. For the first time, Sally bothered to take a good look at the man. Not very tall, thin hair, pudgy, needing a shave. His pale chinos were stained around the crotch. Contemptible individual. Ash had found the sores on the tiger's neck. His lips a hard line, his fingers felt along the ridge of hair showing where the collar had been.

"A shock collar," Sally said. "I found the control in our mate's pocket." She handed Ash a black box with a push button in the middle. If Romero had seen the look in Ash's eyes he would have asked to stay in the cage. The police officer's voice echoed down. "Sir? Everything okay?" "Yes. Have the zoo people set up the cage just outside the front door. Please get all your people outside and onlookers out of the way." "Okay." Sally thought the unseen police officer sounded resigned and maybe reluctant. "I'll have special forces ready to back up if needed." "Call me when you're ready." "Did I interrupt your meeting?" Sally asked. Ash looked downright delectable in an Armani business suit with a conservative tie. Her husband shrugged. "I told them something had come up. These things happen." He grinned. "Although it's not often a tiger in downtown New York." His cell phone chimed and he answered it. "Ready? All right." Sally had Aysha tell the tiger, "We're going from here. Stay close." While Ash ran up the stairs, Sally dug her ruined jeans and shirt out of her backpack and tossed the rags behind the steps where a pile of newspapers, used drink containers and plastic bags had already collected. If the police found the torn clothes, she'd have a hard time explaining. "Bring him up." Ash's voice echoed in the stairwell. Keeping her hand on the tiger's shoulder, Sally walked up the stairs. Ash ran on ahead to open doors. The foyer was empty. The apartment block's front door was open, with a cage set as close as possible to the entrance. They'd rigged planks between the back of a small truck and the top of the apartment's stairs and put a haunch of meat in the cage, along with a bucket. Lights flashed outside but no one was visible on the street. At the sight of the cage, the white tiger hesitated. "Safe," Sally sent to the tiger. "Food. Safe." I'll make sure you're all right, she said in the privacy of her own mind. Sally let the tiger go in by himself, almost running for the meat, and watched him settle with a satisfied growl. She hadn't realized the beast was so thin, his hip bones prominent. The cage door clanged shut, but he barely raised his head from the meat. Sally
wiped the tears from her eyes. On the rooftops, black-clad assault police lowered their guns. Ash slipped an arm around her and hugged her as the truck turned the corner and disappeared.

Chapter 3 ​ "Where are they taking him?" Sally asked. "Bronx zoo, for now," Ash said. "But he can't stay there." She spun around to face him, her damp hair hanging around her face like strings. She had that look on her face, that 'don't mess me about' expression. "Why not?" "It's a white tiger. A genetic mess. It has crossed eyes and probably a host of other faults." Sally folded her arms. "How do you know?" She was going to be stubborn, damn it. Sometimes she could be downright unreasonable. "Because white is a recessive gene, and very rare. A tiger like that wouldn't stand a chance in the wild. They inbreed to get a white tiger, brother to sister, father to daughter. This beast is useless for conservation." Her eyebrows drooped in a little frown that signaled she hadn't thought of that. "Yes. That's obvious. So what will they do with him?" She gasped, a hand outstretched. "Not put him down? The green dream?" She was going to make this difficult. The weretiger rumbled amusement. "It would be kindest. He has a limp, I think perhaps his eyesight is poor, and he looks like he's been starved." Sally grabbed his arm, her blue eyes blazing. "No. I won't have it. He's my tiger. I sat down there in the dark with him with that horrible man. I won't let them kill him unless he's in terrible pain." She stuck out her chin. "And I know he's not." The sound of a man clearing his throat interrupted them. Ash turned to a tall, middle aged man who looked as if he enjoyed fast food more than he should. He held out a hand to Sally. "Lieutenant McCarthy, ma'am. Good to see you okay." "Yes, fine." She smiled up at him. "We'll need to check the backpack, ma'am. Just routine." He held out his hand.

Forcing herself not to swallow, Sally handed him the pack, which he passed on to an underling. "Can you tell me what happened?" McCarthy asked her. "Sure. I was walking past and heard a tiger. We live with tigers in India," she added, taking Ash's arm. "We live beside a tiger reserve," Ash explained. His nerves tingled. He hoped she didn't say too much. "Ah. I see. So you heard the beast?" She nodded. "So I went to see. It might have been injured, or something." "So you released the cat and it attacked Romero." McCarthy spoke mildly, but Ash could almost see the cogs meshing in the man's head. Sally shook her head. "The tiger was free to roam the basement. Romero controlled it with an electrified collar." "It was probably trained from a cub," Ash said. "When the pain is applied, retreat to your cage. Then the pain goes off." "Uh-huh." McCarthy chewed on his lip, letting the silence grow. Say nothing, Sally. Don't fill the vacuum. "And this time it didn't do that?" the policeman finally said. "I took the collar off." As soon as she'd said the words Sally's eyes flashed with anger. "Did you see the sores on its neck? That's... that's..." She spluttered to a halt. "How did Romero get in the tiger's cage?" "He fainted when it attacked, so it left him alone. I dragged him in there for his own safety." "You felt safer with a tiger than a man?" She nodded, sending her dark hair dancing. "Oh, yes. Oh, yes indeed." McCarthy pursed his lips. "Okay. Well, you and Romero were both lucky you came out unscathed. So what can you tell me about the boxes in the basement?" the officer asked. Boxes? This was getting dangerous. Icy fingers crawled down Ash's spine. Be careful. Her gaze was all innocence. "Nothing. I never looked in them." McCarthy's lips jerked in a brief smile. "Not at all?" "No time, Detective." She paused, her expression cool. Then she shrugged. "If I was guessing, I'd say drugs. He had to have some very good reason for keeping a tiger down there. And this is Harlem. You hear the stories, even in Australia."

"Uh-huh." McCarthy was still suspicious. And Ash could hardly blame him. He stared down at Sally for a moment longer. "So you're just guessing?" "That's right. I never touched the boxes." A scuffle at the front door attracted McCarthy's attention. Louis Romero shuffled out between two uniformed police officers, each keeping a firm grip on an arm. Romero caught sight of Sally and glared, his eyes narrowed, until they shoved his head down and forced him into the back of a police car. Sally's lip curled. In Ash's mind, the weretiger growled, "He had best hope he does not meet her again." "You wouldn't have too many tigers in Harlem, would you?" Ash said. McCarthy's gaze snapped back to Ash. "Not often. But it happened before, a few years back. Some fool had a tiger in his apartment, fourth floor, I think it was." Sally's jaw dropped. "Really?" "Oh, yes. A five hundred pound, full grown tiger. Had it from a cub for about three years." "In an apartment? But... what about exercise? And food? Surely somebody noticed." McCarthy's lips curved into a cynical smile. "Nobody sees, nobody knows. He had an alligator up there, too." Ash pushed down his anger. They might be poor specimens of tigers, but no animal deserved to be treated like that. A tiger in an apartment like one of these. Had it ever been outside? Run through grass? Climbed a tree? "What happened to it? The tiger?" Sally asked. "That one? It was sedated and they took it to some place in Ohio, I think. A sanctuary. Some folks said it would never survive, being outdoors after being caged here all those years." "It would not survive in the wild," Ash said. "But in a sanctuary where it did not have to hunt, it would be much, much happier." He waved at the sky. "Air, grass, a pool to play in. Yes, it would cope." McCarthy's cell phone rang. He dug the device out his pocket with a murmured 'excuse me'. He listened, grinned, and said, "Take it in," then put the phone away. "Yes, ma'am, heroin. Millions of dollars worth. That's a great result." The grin faded. "That's sure an interesting story about the tiger. 'Spect you'll be on national television tonight." He jerked his head at the police cordon, where

TV cameras whirred and reporters shouted questions. "We may need to talk to you some more. Contact information?" Ash gave the detective their details. McCarthy raised a hand in salute. "We'll get the backpack back to you. Be seein' you," and joined his own people. "Fuck," Sally said. Ash chuckled. "Now?" "Aw, you know. The news." "Just keep your story consistent. Let me guess the truth. He punished the tiger and your weretiger took over." She flushed. "Yes." He shook his head at her. "You must take care, my love. You don't have control, she could do anything and that could be dangerous for us, as well as other people." "I know," she said in a small voice. "It... just happened, when he zapped the poor tiger a second time, for no reason. Bastard." Ash could remember how hard it was when he was learning to control his alter ego. He put a hand on her shoulder. "But at least she didn't kill. You're getting better." His weretiger chortled, and Ash told him to shut up. Sally hung her head. "Romero fainted." "Ah." And that, of course, had saved his life. Sally would have had a moment to regain control. Just as well she'd taken the change of clothes with her. "What did you do with your clothes?" "Tossed them with the rest of the rubbish at the bottom of the stairs. That policeman's no fool," Sally said, watching McCarthy talking to white-clad forensic types. The danger here was that the police would connect non-existent dots and think Sally had something to do with the drug haul. "Did you touch the boxes?" She shook her head. "They were locked in one of those baggage cages. I never touched it. Romero heard me break in and came down before I had a chance to do anything much." "Well, Officer McCarthy has a result. Let's hope it is sufficient." He thought it would be. McCarthy might have thought he was deadpan, but Ash's tiger sense picked up grim satisfaction. Romero had a history, the police had impounded a huge heroin haul and Romero's only interest in Sally seemed to be a mild recognition of her ability with a tiger. Oh, well. If there were to be more questions, they would come.

The rain had started again, a drizzling mist that caught on his eyelashes. He put an arm around Sally and led her over to the waiting media. Might as well let them have their pictures, and maybe highlight the plight of big, exotic cats in America. "Don't mention any heroin," he told her. The weather turned out to be a blessing. The rain came down harder and the questions were brief. Ash had an idea he knew what the headlines would be. 'Woman fights tiger' or some such nonsense. They tended to emphasize Sally's role in distracting the cat and dragging Romero into the cage. Sally handled it well, oozing modesty and trying to focus on the plight of the white tiger. Finally, when the rain became too much, Ash waved them away. "Thanks, but I want to get my wife out of this weather. Come on, love," Ash put an arm around her shoulders and led her away to wait for a cab. "We have some free time together." He ran his fingers through her wet hair. "Seems to me you could use some warming up." She pushed away from him, just a little. "Careful, I'm all wet. You'll mess your Armani suit." He chuckled. "My Armani suit is all wet, too. That's why they have dry cleaners." She gazed up at him, pleading. "Can we at least go to the zoo? Make sure he's okay?" Ash sighed. "You're not going to let this go, are you?" He didn't even know why he said it. He knew she wasn't going to let the matter rest. And truth be told, he couldn't really blame her. A tiger stuck in a basement for who knew how long? Years? Okay, so the creature wouldn't be part of a conservation program but he didn't deserve... that. The very thought of being stuck in hard, stinking darkness made his flesh crawl. "It's horrible, Ash," Sally said. "I just want to make sure he'll be all right. If I don't, I won't be able to sleep." "That's why I love you. Or one of the reasons. All right, we'll go to the zoo, see how he is." Sally flung her arms around his neck and kissed him. Ash's arms wound around her body, crushing her against him. He loved her so much. She had such strength, such compassion. While they waited for the cab Ash called in a favor with a business associate to connect him to the vet who had been instrumental in bringing the Harlem tiger to the Bronx zoo. Doctor

Bolton was primed to see them when they arrived. A young woman at reception took them around the veterinary hospital, introduced them to the vet and left. Bolton shook hands with both of them. "That tiger owes you, Ms Carter." The vet's voice had a distinct Southern twang. "I could kill those bastards. Down in that stinking, filthy basement as a guard cat for God knows how long." He shook his head. "Sometimes you wonder who the animals are." Wasn't that a fact. "How is he?" Sally asked. "Still coming to. We sedated him to check him. Want to see him?" She nodded. Ash swallowed his grin. Bolton led them into a closed-off area containing a row of cages on a concrete floor. The place had the medical smell of disinfectant. A serval with a bandaged hindleg crouched in a corner of one cage, a cougar lay asleep in another. The white tiger lay with its head resting on its paws. The great head raised slightly as they approached and he managed a snarl. He still looked groggy, but that was to be expected. "He is sleepy," the weretiger said. "But happy to not have the thing around his neck." "What's his condition?" Ash asked the vet. "He's underweight and his elbows are enlarged from lying on concrete all the time. He has a cleft palate and crooked forelegs." Bolton gazed at Ash, his eyes hard. "You know about this stuff, don't you? Curtis says you run a tiger reserve in India." "I don't run it, no. The Government runs the parks. But my family used to own the land, so I have a deep interest in the tigers, and the people who live around the park. If you're asking me if I know about the genetic manipulation to breed a white tiger, the answer is yes." Bolton nodded. "And this poor beast is the result. We're trying to get better legislation but that's difficult." "And this cat? He'll be going to a sanctuary?" Sally asked. Bolton frowned, his gaze fixed on the ground. "No. I'm sorry." He shrugged. "It costs, you see. I thought they'd be able to take him at Wild Sanctuary, but funds are tight." He caught his lip between his teeth. "He's old. I'm really sorry." Sally's face crumpled and she squeezed her eyes shut. "After all he's been through, he's just going to be killed?" When she opened

her eyes again, a single tear slid down her cheek. "I'm prepared to pay for transport," Ash said, "and contribute to the cat's well being. And his medical expenses." Bolton glanced between them. "You're talking a lot of money, sir." "Yes. I can afford it. If that's what my wife wants." Beaming, Sally squeezed his arm. "I'm prepared to forgo my dress allowance for a few years." Dress allowance? She didn't have a dress allowance. She hadn't wanted one. Bolton was no fool. Bedraggled they might be, but Ash could sense the man sizing up the suit he was wearing. "Let me make some phone calls." He walked away, leaving them with the tiger, who warbled a rolling growl. "He is confused, and frightened. This place smells," Ash's weretiger said. Sally pushed her fingers through the links in the tiger's cage. He moved to her, and pressed his head against her hand. "He trusts me," she murmured. "I have to make sure he's all right." She turned her blue, baby tiger eyes to Ash and his heart melted. Of course the tiger trusted her. "I know it's going to be a lot of money. But I can't just leave him here. I can't." "I know, Sally. We'll find somewhere for him." "Good news," Bolton said from the doorway. Sally took her hand away and the tiger raised his head, staring at the intruder, his lips curled. "There's a place in North Carolina prepared to take him, if you're prepared to finance him." Ash simply nodded. "Do they want a deposit, or do I simply write a check for one hundred thousand?" Bolton pushed his glasses up his nose and grinned. "They can get a carrier here the day after tomorrow." "I'll go with him," Sally said. "There's no need ma'am, he'll be—" "I'll go with him." Bolton took a half-step backwards, his eyes wide. "Sorry." Sally raised her hands, palms out, pushing down. "I didn't mean to yell. I'm a bit tense about it all." In his mind Ash's weretiger rumbled his amusement. "Well. I'll, er, let them know. Can I call you with a time?"

Ash gave the vet his cell phone number and asked him to call them a cab. On the way back to the hotel, Sally squeezed his knee. "Thanks. You don't mind?" He put his arm around her and drew her close. "Of course not. I take it you've had enough of New York?" "Yup. Nice to visit, but not my scene at all. I'm over cities." "Mmm. Me, too. But..." He shrugged. It was part of his job, part of what he had to do to keep the money coming in. The taxi slowed and rolled to a halt at a traffic light. Ahead, the skyscrapers of Manhattan sparkled in their early evening light show. They called it the concrete jungle and it was true. There were far more dangers roaming around there than in the green jungle of home. "Sally, you go with the tiger to its new home. I'll finish my business here and come and join you. I haven't seen much of America beyond New York and Los Angeles. We can hire a four wheel drive and have a look around for a week or two. That honeymoon we never had. What do you say?"

Chapter 4 ​ DAVE GARDNER'S GAZE grazed over the heads of the people sitting around the tables in the bar room and homed in on the curved bar with its row of wooden, high-backed bar stools. McCarthy was there, as he expected, perched in his favorite place near the corner. Damn, Bobby's was busy this evening. Gardner edged his way between the tables and wedged himself against the bar next to McCarthy. "How're you doin' Joe?" McCarthy grinned and finished his beer. "Why am I not surprised to see you?" Gardner raised a finger. Johnny, the regular bartender, ambled over, polishing a glass with a towel. "Hiya Dave. The usual?" "Yes, and whatever Joe wants." "Bourbon and coke," Joe said. Johnny nodded and reached for glasses. Gardner watched him drop in ice, then draw double shots from the dispenser. It always seemed a shame to Gardner, ruining good liquor by mixing it with coke. But to each his own. Johnny kept his eyes on McCarthy's face as he poured in the mixer, until the cop nodded. Gardner poured his own dash of water from a jug, then lifted the glass. "Cheers, Joe. Good result." McCarthy's thin face split in a wide grin. "Oh, yes. Thank you, mama." He took a big slurp from his glass. "Got a minute? Over there?" Gardner said, jerking his head at a free booth. McCarthy eased out of his chair. "Sure. Long as you're buying." They picked their way between the patrons and slid onto vinyl benches around a laminex table sticky with spilled beer. A half- eaten bowl of peanuts took up space in the middle. Gardner ignored it, McCarthy dug out a handful of nuts. "So what can you tell me?" Gardner asked.

When he'd finished chewing, McCarthy said, "A tiger was kept in a basement to guard a haul of heroin." "Aw, come on, Joe. That's not special. Everybody knows that. Whose heroin?" McCarthy's fingers tapped on his glass. "Easy enough to guess. We think – think! Chuck Cusmano may be involved." Gardner threw a mouthful of bourbon down his throat, savoring the cold of ice and the warmth of liquor. Yes! He'd been chasing Cusmano for months, chasing the respectable businessman who was really a crime baron. "Is there anything to link the heroin to Cusmano?" McCarthy waved a finger, leaning over the table at him. "No. We got no proof, Dave. But there's a connection with Louis Romero from way back. His last time in the slammer was from working for Chucky. He seemed to have gone straight after that. Or so we thought." "So why has it taken so long to find this stash? Would have thought you'd follow up on him." "Uh-huh. We did. Hey, sometimes folks make mistakes." By the set of McCarthy's jaw, this line of enquiry was finished. Which probably meant a bent cop. "What about the woman and her husband?" McCarthy leaned back against the seat, his hand cradling the empty glass. "What about them? She's an Australian medical doctor, never been to the States before, no record. He's an Indian business tycoon. Been here many times but has no record. There's a hint he does business with Triad-related businessmen in Hong Kong, but nothing substantial. They're heavily involved in tiger conservation in India." "But what's the story? She just walks in and finds a tiger, and that's okay? It doesn't hurt her? Come on Joe. It's bullshit, has to be." "Why?" "I saw she had a backpack. What about that?" "A purse, makeup in a little bag, sun glasses, bottle of water, tissues, sweets, some brochures. No sign of drugs, and none of her prints on anything but the collar and the door. She's not involved, Dave." Gardner spread his hands. "A half starved tiger? Just lets her walk in? What did Romero say?"

"What she said. The tiger jumped him." McCarthy stopped and stared down at his empty glass. Gardner took the hint and whistled up a waitress. "Same again, honey." "Romero isn't too sure exactly what happened," McCarthy said. "It was dark. The light switch didn't work. As a matter of fact, the bulb was broken. We found the glass on the floor. Romero said he used the electric collar on the tiger, it was backing off, then something happened, and he was flat on his back with a tiger snarling down at him." "So what are you saying? The tiger didn't take him down?" The waitress set down the new drinks, slopping McCarthy's only slightly. She skimmed a cloth over the tabletop, distributing the stickiness a little more evenly. "The tiger must've taken him down. They found tiny marks on his chest where the claws had stuck through the material." He grinned. "I guess having a five hundred pound cat sitting on your chest would affect your memory banks, as well as causing you to shit yourself." True. He would have done the same, he was sure. "Did Romero say where he got the tiger?" McCarthy shook his head. "Said it was there when he got the job three years or so ago. The guy who employed him was a fella called Turner." He shrugged. "No trace, needless to say." Dead ends. More fucking dead ends. "How did he say he got into the cage?" "He woke up in there." "And she dragged him? She's—what—five-five, five-six? With a jumpy tiger on the loose?" McCarthy slumped over his bourbon and coke. His eyes had half-closed, like shutters. "It's amazing what people can do when they have to." Gardner shook his head. It just didn't make sense. "Do you believe that's what happened?" McCarthy took another long swig of his drink, sat back and scratched his nose. "Wanna know what, Dave? I don't give a shit. We got us a huge haul of heroin, Romero's given us a couple leads, and the tiger's gone to a better place. That's result with a capital R. Case closed." Gardner's heart thumped. "They killed the tiger?"

"Naw. It was taken to Bronx zoo. The last one went to a sanctuary. This one probably will, too. If you happen to care. Which I don't." He peered at Gardner through narrowed eyes. "What's your take?" "I'm not sure." Gardner stared into his glass. "A hunch, I guess." Sometimes fate did strange things. "I just have a feeling this tiger has something to do with Cusmano." McCarthy drained the rest of the contents of the glass and pushed himself to his feet. "Know what I think, Dave? I think you need to take a step back. You've become obsessed and you can't see the wood for the trees anymore. Why'n you take a break? Cusmano'll be here when you get back." He waved a hand and meandered a little unsteadily to the exit. Gardner drained his liquor and slammed the glass down on the tabletop. McCarthy was right, damn it. He'd become obsessive, seeing Cusmano in every roll, every rattle of the dice. Why did he think this business with the tiger was so strange? Apart from the obvious, of course. What did he think? That she was a drug courier? Picking up or putting down? Maybe. Why not? People always said follow the money trail and those two sure had money. A few million bucks worth of heroin in Harlem stank of Cusmano. There had to be a link. There had to be. The apartment where the tiger drama had taken place was only a few blocks away. The forensics unit would have been all over that basement but Gardner felt an urge to take a look for himself. You never knew. His hands shoved into his pockets, he walked the few blocks to the brownstone. Now the cops were gone it was just another Harlem apartment block, no different to its neighbors. Gardner ran up the steps into the foyer. He paused for a moment to orient himself and find the door to the stairs. The stink of urine when he opened the door had him reaching for a handkerchief. His eyes streaming, the handkerchief clamped to his nose, he paced down the steps. The light at the bottom had been left on, illuminating the yellowed newspaper, fast food containers and rags. The door to the cellar stood ajar. His heart thundering, Gardner's footsteps slowed, the sound deadened in the heavy air. The reek was almost visible, a foul mix of urine, feces and wild beast. And darkness. It seemed to trickle around the door, pooling on the floor. Why was he so frightened? The room was empty. Or at least, the drugs and the tiger were gone. He reached out and pushed the door,

which creaked open on damaged hinges. She'd forced the door, McCarthy said. Nothing. Just a filthy maw where a tiger had eked out an existence for years. That was what happened to drug addicts, too. An image came back, of a filthy alley stinking of cat, and a body... Gardner rubbed his face with both hands. McCarthy was right. He was getting obsessive, needing a break. Maybe a story about the pretty Australian doctor and an abused tiger would sell to the women's magazines? Yeah. He'd go ask for an interview before every other bastard in this town got there first. Who knows? He might be able to find out where that tiger came from. GARDNER WATCHED SALLY Carter duck out of the underground garage of the hotel and congratulated himself. Let the others hang around in the foyer with their cameras and microphones. He'd taken one look at the media pack and searched around for alternatives. Of course, she might not have gone anywhere at all, but that was always a chance a reporter took, and on a lovely day like this, who'd want to hang around indoors? She stood at the curb like a greyhound at a start, waiting for a chance to dash across the road. The traffic thinned and off she went, running with a long, loping stride. Gardner put his cell phone back into his pocket and followed the figure in anonymous jeans and a blue tee-shirt, a backpack slung over one shoulder. She was headed for Central Park. Inside the gates she stopped and sucked in deep breaths. He took the chance to catch up to her. "Sally Carter?" Her eyebrows shot up and her gaze flicked over him. "You're mistaken." She turned and strolled up the road, ignoring him. "I know you've had enough of reporters," he said, keeping pace with her. "I'm not Sally Carter. I just look a bit like her." She made to walk on. "You look a lot like her and you have that same Australian accent." She tutted. "Leave me alone or I'll call a cop." She began to run, employing that long stride which ate up the ground. Damn, he hadn't had to work so hard since he'd run in college athletics. "Sally, please. I want to write a story about the tiger, not

you," he said, keeping pace with her. She stopped so suddenly he had to jog back. Her eyes were amazing, a sort of smoky blue that saw right through you. "You want to write about the tiger?" "That's right." He nodded, panting. "The tiger. How it was kept and how it will live now. A feel-good story." She lifted one side of her lip. "Happy endings, huh? So what do you need from me?" "Where is he going? When? Can I go with him?" She gazed at him for a long moment while his heart settled down to a reasonable rate. "You could have asked them at the Bronx Zoo. I expect you have." He felt the flush rise into his cheeks. "I wanted your permission." She laughed, those blue eyes sparkling with mirth. "What's your name?" He fumbled for his press card. "Dave Gardner," he said, handing her the ID. She read it carefully. "Free lance." She handed the card back. "There are a lot of neglected, abused tigers in this country. Or so I've heard." It would only encourage these... these... bastards to get another litter to abuse. Do you see?" Her eyes were too bright. "Yes, I think so." He reached for another muffin, not so much because he was hungry, but for something to do. "I can do a lot better than give you a list," she said, leaning over the table toward him again. Gardner concentrated on her eyes. Don't look down. Don't. Look. Down. He swallowed a piece of muffin. "Uh... yeah?" "What about if I show you one of these petting malls? You can see for yourself. And maybe get a few pictures." "Fantastic. When can we do that?" "I saw an ad yesterday. They're setting up a display down at the mall in Coopersville the day after tomorrow." Jill snorted. "Have

your picture taken with the king of the jungle. Huh." She shoved a sheet under his nose. Gardner gazed down at an advertising sheet showing three cute pictures of kids with cubs on their laps, and a couple of close ups of cubs. 'Pet a tiger.' Down the bottom it noted 'cubs for sale'. "Hey," he said, pointing at the picture of a cub. "This tiger has blue eyes." Jill leaned over to look. He caught a whiff of roses. "Oh, yeah. All cubs have blue eyes. They turn yellow when they get older. Except for the white ones. Their eyes stay blue." Another thing he'd learned. Now where had he seen that shade of blue recently? Ulysses? Must have been. 'Day after tomorrow' was much more important. He'd have to get an extension at the motel. He'd have to put the bill on his credit card, too, and he already owed the bank too much money. "Is that going to be a problem?" Jill sat with her hands folded on her lap, the tip of her tongue protruding between her lips. "What? The timing? Uh... no. No, it'll be okay. I'll have to extend my booking at the motel." He dug his cell phone out of his pocket and rang the motel. The proprietor was apologetic but the rooms were all taken. "No dice, huh?" Jill said as he put the phone away. "Not there. Is there anywhere else? Not too pricey? Not too far away?" He felt inadequate. She'd be comparing him to Bhosle, who wasn't all that much older than him, handsome, debonair, rolling in cash and great with tigers. "You can stay at my place," she offered. "I don't have a spare bed, but there's the couch." Gardner's heart jolted. "Are you sure?" She nodded. "You're going to write an article about tigers for a national women's magazine. I'm sure I can do my bit to help." National women's magazine. Goddam. He had no idea if he could sell the story at all. He'd just muttered words to Sally Carter, who must have passed them on, but with a bit more impact. Chinese whispers. He thought briefly about admitting the half-truth but thought better of it. What the hell? Maybe he could sell a good article to a women's magazine. Especially if he could nail Chucky Cusmano along the way. "Well, that'd be great. Thanks. Awesome." He found himself grinning like a kid.

She sagged in her chair, smiling, almost as though she was afraid he'd say no. "I've got some chores to attend to. I finish at four. Want to come back then?" "Chores here? Can I help?" "SHEESH," GARDNER SIGHED as he pulled off the borrowed rubber boots. "Is it always like that?" Never mind. He'd find a chance to talk to her about drugs. But what he wanted right now was a bourbon and coke, easy on the coke. And some food. A steak sounded good. "Oh shit," hissed Jill. "There's Mom. Tell her I've gone to admin." She slipped away. He straightened up and found himself staring at Barbara Kranstein. "Ms. Kranstein. Barbara. How are you?" "I'm fine. I'm surprised to see you here." Her eyebrows were raised, asking the question. "I thought I'd do a day as a volunteer. All background for the story, you know? Adds authenticity." "I'm sure it does. She stopped, took a notebook out of her bag and scribbled. "Here's the address and my number if you get lost," she said, handing him a sheet torn from the notebook. "I'll see you shortly." Gardner saw the Civic drive away before he reached his Jeep. He typed the address into his navigation system and set off, following the instructions provided by the standard male voice. He'd toyed with the idea of loading Homer Simpson but at the end of the day, was it worth the expense? Jill lived in Coopersville, a forty minute drive away. Gardner passed a shopping mall and wondered if that was where the cubs

would be displayed. The voice told him to turn right in five hundred yards, down a leafy street lined with houses that had probably been up market, once. Now, judging by the mailboxes out front, they had been divided into apartments. Sally lived in one of the less forlorn looking houses. She was waiting for him, standing in the front door. He carried his overnight bag into her front room. Big cats were everywhere. Posters stuck on the walls, a leopard motif throw almost covering a threadbare couch, tiger cushions on chairs that had seen better days. She laughed. "I bet you think I'm obsessed." Gardner sat down on the couch and bounced. A bit lumpy but he'd slept on worse. "You do seem to have a bit of a fixation. Like your mom." "Coffee?" "I'd love one." He walked through a room barely large enough for a double bed, a dresser and a wardrobe. A picture of a tiger splashing through water hung above the bed. He picked up the one with the lion on it and sipped. The coffee tasted metallic, like the bottom of a kettle. He pulled a face and instantly regretted it. She drooped. "Yeah. I need a new kettle." I was looking through the brochures at the motel. They had an ad for a place called Billy Jo's. Said they had music?" "I have to be at work at ten."

"Gives us a few hours. Come on. It'll be fun." BILLY JO'S WAS AN OLD house refurbished as a restaurant. Gardner elected to sit out on the verandah, overlooking an old garden filled with flowering shrubs and the sound of cicadas. Maybe if he eased around it, he could get her to talk. "Latin Quarter?" "I spent some time there, yes. And Turtle Cove." "It's a fun place. Do you like jazz?" She smiled, lighting up her face. "The old stuff, yes. Miles Davis, Ella Fitzgerald, Lena Horn, Satchmo." He knew all those, too. They talked, ordered dessert, enjoyed ice cream sundaes. said, shaking his head. "I..." He wanted to tell her about Suzie but the words wouldn't come, the memories too recent, too raw, his guilt an oozing wound in his conscience. Chapter 9 ​ "STOP WHERE YOU CAN," Sally said, laying a hand on Ash's arm. "I have to get a picture of this view." The road skirted up a steep slope, giving spectacular views over a tree-covered valley to successive ranges of hills. Ash pulled the SUV off the road. Sally set up her tripod while he admired the scenery. Dark pines rose nearby, their spiky limbs standing out against the bluish tinge of the mountains on the other side of the valley. Beyond, the further peaks had faded to purple. He could see why his wife would want a photo of this particular vista. He stretched, enjoying the cooler mountain air and the deafening silence. What an amazing place the Appalachian Trail had turned out to be. Rolling farmland, forests, peaks, babbling streams, waterfalls. They'd seen deer. Sally would have hundreds of pictures to sort when she got home. "There's a river down there," Sally called from her perch on a rock. "I just saw a glint of water." The two beasts were drinking, the sun's rays sparkling on their coats, while behind them the waterfall gleamed like crystal. She rested her arms on the car door. "I wouldn't mind a shot like that." been able to do that since they arrived in the US. He missed it as much as she did, loping through the forest, silent and effortless. "Probably best if we didn't meet any deer, love." Long shadows fell across the road, turning it into a visual railway track of bright and dark lines. The track ended suddenly, widening into an empty parking lot. A toilet block off to the left was the only building. As in every parking area, this one had signs warning people not to leave food in reach of raccoons and bears. Ash drove past the 'no camping' sign and parked near the well-marked trail to the waterfall. With the engine switched off all he could hear was the subtle gurgle of the nearby river, hidden by the undergrowth. Sally went around to the back of the vehicle and started pulling out the camping gear. "Seems a good time to get something to eat. I'm hungry." "What have we got?" Ash asked, helping her with the stove. "Sausages," she said, pulling the packet out of the travel fridge. "And there's tomatoes, cheese, onions. And... a loaf of bread." Ash summoned better eyesight and hearing from his weretiger self and found where the bird perched on the edge of the parking area.

"Time to go for a run?" Sally asked. She'd begun to tidy, packing away the gas bottle and the little stove, putting trash in a bag. Ash helped her, then locked the vehicle. "Let's practice changing a few times," he said. Ash concentrated, letting the barrier between him and the weretiger dissipate. "You know what I want to do?" he said to his alter ego. "We did this the other day. Swap positions, but not exactly where you are." "Yes. That way I keep my clothes." "Huh. Clothes. Stupid. Why you bother is beyond me. You take them off to bathe, shit, mate." "Thank you for your commentary. Are you ready?" The beast shook his head. "Tch. Of course." Reality blurred and shifted in a way that used to leave him dizzy and now he could see his human self as if through dirty glass while his mind rode in the weretiger's skin. other, fading from recent to a week. All the while Sally matched him, a breath behind. The scent of the river drew closer and its sound changed to a whispering rush, underpinned with a dull, murmuring roar which had to be the waterfall. Dark water rushed over two spills divided by an island spur of bare rock. The deep roar of the main fall, the reedy rush of the rapids, the tiny tinkles of falling droplets. "Fancy a swim?" he asked. A chorus came back from his weretiger and his mate. Yes, a swim would be lovely. He jumped easily back to the bank, aware of Sally behind him, then headed along the rocky path down to the base of the falls. If he'd been human the trail would have been a slippery scramble over jutting outcrops and water-scoured ruts. As a tiger he did the journey in half a dozen elegant bounds, ending with a totally inelegant belly flop into the pool. A wave of happiness

coursed through him as he swam, shaking his head to clear the water away. Sally surged in after him, intent on grabbing his tail in her jaws. He wheeled around, trying to get his tail out of the way but the water slowed the movement down. Her teeth took hold. "Ow. Not so hard." She let go immediately, but she chortled with laughter. "Shouldn't leave it hanging about like that." She'd swum off across the pool. "You're not going to let her get away with that?" the weretiger rumbled in disbelief. "Idiot," she complained edging away under the trees. A deer trail angled off into the trees. Ash caught the scent in his nostrils. "Prey," whispered the weretiger. "No. Don't even think about," Ash snapped. "You too, Sally. Tell her no. We can't hunt here." The big black cat that was Sally swayed, shifting her weight from foot to foot. Sally/ Aysha's head drooped and her tail began to swish. "Thanks," she said. "Running would be good. But not down there." No. Not down there. Ash found another animal track going downstream and trotted along that, pushing his body along a trail meant for a much smaller creature. When he reached a ford that was clearly a vehicle crossing he turned up away from the river. "Race you to the top." The moon had risen by the time Sally had had enough. Ash

wasn't in a hurry to admit it, but he was become a little fatigued himself. The run had been fun and exhilarating, encountering different smells, different tracks. "No," Ash said. "No, I think anybody turning up here, now, may well be up to no good." A loud thump split the air. "Try again. It splintered." The voice was loud and surly.
