"I know, I know. I can't fix the American animal system. It makes me sick. What now?" He shrugged. "Sleep in the back of the car for tonight. We can get the window fixed in the morning." Sally woke before dawn, to the sound of bird song. Grey, pre- dawn light brightened the sky. Dawn. Her heart bounced. That was why they were here, after all, to photograph the waterfall at dawn. If she could make it down that steep, rocky trail in her human form. Ash lay on his back, snoring gently. She flexed her foot under the sleeping bag. It didn't feel too bad. The real test would come when she put some weight on the wound. "It heals well," Aysha said. "It is clean." She shook Ash, who sat up, blinking his eyes. "What's the time?" He glanced outside and groaned. "Sally..." "That's why we're here, surely? To photograph the waterfall at dawn?" He'd fallen back down again, staring at the ceiling. "It's cold. And your foot is injured." "Come on, Ash. We can at least try." Sally eased herself out of the sleeping bag and reached for her jeans. Dressed, she slid out onto the ground. Now was the big test. She put her weight on her left foot. Not too bad. One step, then another. "Walk properly, Sally." Ash finished pulling on a sweatshirt. She strode and winced. Damn. This wasn't going to work. Ash didn't say anything, just shook his head. "Let's find some breakfast." He started toward the driver's seat. Damn it. If they left, that was it. She wouldn't get another chance. "I have four legs," Aysha said. "Ash," she called. "We can go down as tigers. We'll get there really quickly and I won't have to carry my gear." He stared at her. "If I have hold of my camera gear when I change, I'll end up over there with my gear, won't I?" It made sense to her. If your clothes could transfer, why not whatever you carried? Ash gaped, rather like a goldfish. "You'll still have a sore foot. Paw." "Yes, but I'll have four legs so I can favor one. Oh, come on, Ash. We won't be coming back here any time soon." "Okay," he said at last. "It's worth a try." Frowning he wagged a finger at her. "But we have to be careful. If someone turns up, it

could get difficult." "We'll be careful." Grinning like a loon, she dragged out her camera gear and slung the bag over her shoulders. That sickening dizziness hit her and then she stood on the bitumen, swishing her tail. The camera gear was gone, over there with her body. The look on Ash's face was priceless, a mix of astonishment and admiration. Then his outline blurred and the big black tiger faced her. "Quickly now." He bounded off to the trail down to the waterfall's base. Sally followed, keeping her weight off the left hind foot, leaping from rock to rock. Balanced on the rocks at the base of the waterfall, she concentrated again – and there she stood with her camera bag slung over her shoulder. She punched the air, releasing the exhilaration. To the east a glimmer of sun had appeared above the trees. Sally set up her tripod, ready for the show as the light crept down the face of the falls, turning the rockface to gold and the water to flowing silver. A picture of deer drinking would be nice. Ash had taken the opportunity to go swimming as a tiger, out of range of her viewfinder. In her head he said, "We'd better go". She agreed, dismantling the tripod, putting the gear away. One last picture. Ash climbed out of the pool, a huge black beast, the water shining on his ebony coat. She couldn't resist. The photo would be magnificent, she thought to herself as she stowed the camera. Changed back to Aysha's form, she and Ash leaped up the trail to the car park. Just before they reached the entrance Ash said, "Oops," and dived into the bushes. People. Sally heard a car door slam, a child's voice. The urge to change came too fast. Slow down, slow down. The human Sally caught hold of a tree trunk to regain her balance, aware of Aysha's derisive snort. "Okay?" Ash asked, frowning in concern. "Yes." Sally limped out of the bushes, grabbing at her torn shirt. A woman standing with a man and a boy at the top of the path started, her hand rising to her mouth, her eyes wide. Sally smiled. "Hi. It's beautiful down there, but it's not an easy walk." The relief on the woman's face was palpable. "You gave me such a fright." Sally laughed. "Sorry." She shared a grin with Ash. "Not half as
much of a fright as she might have had," she added as the woman disappeared down the trail.

Chapter 11 ​ "AWRIGHT AWRIGHT." GARDNER sat up slowly. Lord, he felt rotten. Every single lump in this godforsaken sofa had imprinted on his back. He prized open caked lashes and blinked at Jill, standing over him with her arms folded. "Wassa time?" "Time you were up. We're off to have our photo taken with a tiger cub, remember?" Bright light lanced through the window. Damn. It must be near on lunchtime. Rubbing a hand over his stubble, Gardner sat up. "I thought you were mad at me. I thought you wouldn't want to go—" "So you bought yourself a bottle of whiskey and got wasted." She pushed with her toe at a bottle lying on the carpet next to the sofa. "Sorry." His mouth felt like the inside of a parrot's cage and something was playing a bass drum in his head. She stood in front of him, arms folded, staring down at him. "Yeah, I'm sorry, too. He ignored the little voice that mentioned he might find the lady quite attractive, too. She was waiting for an answer, frowning at him through her glasses. He nodded. "Okay. Just the cats." She replied with a curt nod and went into the kitchen. He picked up the dark glass bottle beside the sofa and sloshed it. Not even half full. Shit. He heard the clatter of a cup, the click of a toaster being pushed down. "Want your coffee black?" she called. "Yeah." He pulled himself upright and searched around for his jeans. She had her hand out, complaining to the photographer. "How can we get a decent picture of Ryan with that happening? How about you switch cubs with one of those?" She pointed at the cage.

An attendant took the wriggling cub from the child's lap, then she blew in its face. Suddenly placid, the cub was returned to Ryan, who beamed at the photographer. "Well, that worked," Gardner said. "Huh. Of course it fucking did." Jill's voice was a growl. "That's what a mother does to a cub to discipline it. Poor little fella has been told he's bad." "Sure, but it worked." She turned on him, hands on hips. "He hasn't got a fucking mother. He's just got these bitches." Gardner took her arm. "Settle down, honey, or we won't get anywhere." "It makes me furious," she growled. "Come on. We need intelligence, not a fight." He though she was going to argue, her body stiff with rage. He stared into her eyes until her head tilted and her shoulders sagged. "Okay." Together, they joined the end of the queue. "They're so cute," cooed the woman in front of them. "How old are they?" Ignoring Jill's look of disgust, Gardner switched off the camera. Another man, similarly dressed, stood on the other side of the fenced-off area. They'd sure brought in the

heavies for not much. This sort of security for half a dozen cubs? "They're for sale." Despite their best efforts, he couldn't miss the sunken frame, the hollow cheeks. Not like the pretty little girl in her prom dress, whirling around in the living room for him to admire. And he'd left her. Left her to her own devices, for some scumbag to take advantage of her. A hand touched his arm. Jill gazed up at him with wide, brimming eyes full of understanding and pleading for forgiveness. "I didn't know." He sighed. "Yeah. Well now you do. It wasn't so long ago. She was only nineteen. Just a kid." The anger welled again and he clenched his fist. "I want to get the bastard that did that to her. Not the poor sap of a pusher who was probably as much a victim as she was. The big boss, the one with the big house and the fancy cars." He looked away, at the wall, the sky, the parking lot: anywhere, while around him a woman pushed a baby carriage into the mall, a family came out with their groceries, a kid whined about wanting fries. "Sorry." Jill's head was bent. She looked small, contrite. Gardner felt stupid. He slipped an arm around the girl's thin shoulders and hugged her against him. "Come on, babe. Let's find some coffee and then see what we're going to do about those bastards." He led her back into the mall, heading down another aisle from where the pet photography was happening, keeping that grip on her body, hoping she wouldn't pull away. The local coffee store wasn't crowded. Gardner gave Jill his camera and directed her to find a booth at the back. Carrying the two large lattes on a tray, he slipped onto the bench opposite her. He'd bought donuts, too, the sweet smell of cinnamon mixing with the coffee. He took a large bite, savoring the sugar. Jill fiddled with the takeaway mug, sipping a little, running her finger along the edge as though it were bone china, sipping a little more. He watched her from under his eyelashes while he drank. She was stewing on something. He could wait. This was journalist mode. Get the interviewee to do the talking. "So why are you interested in the tigers?" She didn't look at him. "You're not, are you?" She gazed up at him then, her disappointment obvious in her expression and the sag of her shoulders. Gardner took a deep breath and let it out. Damn it. He was. And he was interested in her. "I'm... not. That is, I wasn't. I didn't know.

Now I've seen what happens, yes, I'm interested. And I will write that story." She pushed the half empty cup away and rested her elbows on the tabletop. "Has this got something to do with your sister?" He rested his chin on his fist. "Maybe. He felt numb. She wasn't as silly... no, that was the wrong word. Focused? One eyed? As he'd thought. Her demeanor changed in an instant. She drained her coffee in a few gulps and sat bolt upright. "So what do we do now?" "Um... I'd like some more photos of the people running the operation, especially the security guards." She grinned. "You'll have to do that yourself. I guess I'm off the Christmas card list with them." Gardner chuckled with her. "Maybe I should go and get a disguise of some sort, pop into the variety store here." Gardner stared at her. She was like a chameleon, full of fire and brimstone and stupidity in one moment and cool and calculating the next. "We want to try to find out where they come from, don't we?" she asked. "Nose around their truck a bit?" "What about money?" She shrugged. "All it needs is a change of shirt and a hair band. I've done it before." She caught her lip in her teeth. I'll meet you back at the car in ten."

They slid out of the booth and made their way past the few tables with patrons, back into the mall. Jill headed off to the variety store. Gardner slung the camera over his shoulder and set his cell phone. He'd done this before, too. Pretend to talk on the phone while he took photographs. They might not be as good as his DSLR, but phone pictures were pretty damn good these days. Certainly good enough to find out if his friends at NYPD recognized anybody. Gardner sauntered past the petting display, aware of eyes on his back. He pulled out the phone and turned around, talking as if to a friend. As he turned, he snapped the big man with the shades. And again. The man's head turned, probably looking for Jill. Another picture. Laughing as if at a joke, Gardner moved on to target the other goon. This was good. One of the attendants went to talk to the guard. Gardner took a picture. Then a few more of the whole setup. "Yeah, gotta go. Catch you later, okay?" He put the phone away and strolled back past the fenced off area, where a kid of about twelve was holding up a mewling tiger cub by its front paws. Gardner suppressed the surge of irritation. He must be getting it bad. Jill, wearing sunglasses, was waiting for him, lounging against the car. She wore blue slacks and a light blue shirt in a subtle check pattern, and she'd pinned on a name tag that said 'Cheryl'. Her hair was tied back in a ponytail, held with a red scrunchy. "Who's Cheryl?" he asked. She smiled. "A member of staff I don't like. This is what the cleaners here wear. Did you get your photos?" Wow. Smarter and smarter. She would just blend in with the rest of the staff. He waved the cell phone. "Now we find the truck they came in." He unlocked the Jeep. "They'll have parked around the back." She waved an arm, indicating the direction, where a cement fence overhung with trees marked the boundary of the property. "I work here, remember?" Gardner's heart warmed again. They were in this together. The distance of yesterday had disappeared like a passing shower. He hoped. "What's the best place to park to get a look at the vehicle without being noticed?" "Round in the staff parking area. Hop in. I'll direct." She slid into the car. He eased the Jeep out of the bay, following the cars heading for the exit. Jill had him turn right, around to the back of the complex, well away from the shops. From where he stopped, Gardner could

see a row of trucks, some backed up to a loading ramp. Nothing stood out, no colorful posters like on the Tiger Territory trucks. "I'll take a look." Jill opened the door. Gardner grasped her arm, making her pause. "Take it easy, okay? Those bruisers out there didn't look like they'd worry about a bit of violence." "Don't worry. I'm just a cleaner fetching a bin." She closed the door softly and walked away. Feeling guilty, Gardner watched her every step. She was a nice kid. He didn't want to be the cause of her getting hurt. Not like Suzie. Time passed. He'd already rolled down the window to let in some air, and checked the pictures on the cell phone. Not brilliant, but good enough for a police check. Two of the trucks had started up and left, rumbling past the Jeep on the way to the main road where the rush hour traffic had just begun to build. He looked at his watch for the hundredth time. He was just about to go looking for her when Jill rounded the corner of the building. His head drooped against the car seat, he closed his eyes and let out a great, soughing sigh of relief. He reached across and opened the car door for her before she arrived. "Just around the corner. It's a cube van that probably was used for horses. It's done a few miles. I hung around for a while, chatted to one of the mall's security guys out having a smoke. They're due to pack up at 7:30pm." "Great. Let's find a burger somewhere and come back later. I don't know about you, but I'm dying for a toilet break." He took off the handbrake and turned the key. They found a fast food restaurant and claimed a booth with a curved bench seat to while away the time. Jill leaned toward him over the table. "So tell me. We follow them and then what?" Gardner pulled another French fry out of the paper packet. He hadn't thought much beyond following them, finding out where they went. "Then we find out what tiger farm they go to. I'm assuming that's what they'll do, return to their operating base. Then we can find out if Cusmano... or, should I say, we find out who's behind the operation. I'm hoping Sally Carter will help with that." Jill's smile lit up her face. "She's nice, isn't she? And her husband..." She waggled her eyebrows. "What a hunk. Yum." Yeah, well. A hunk with a mountain of money. He pushed aside

his irritation. It wasn't as if he was jealous. "I think he quite fancies his wife, don't you?" Jill laughed. "I didn't think I was in the running, if that's what you're thinking." Gardner felt stupid. Was he so transparent? "Amazing how good she was with Ulysses, wasn't it?" They do get to know their handlers and can be quite friendly, even if they haven't seen the people for ages. But even so, yes, I'd say she was special." Jill giggled. "As well as being very pretty?" Gardner cleared his throat. Yep, that transparent. "Looks like we can both look, huh?" Jill's wide smile brightened her face. "It seemed to me they were pretty wrapped up with each other. I'll bet they haven't been married long." Gardner decided to forget about Sally Carter's mysterious affinity with tigers. After all, what did he care? All he wanted was Cusmano. And if he took down a tiger breeding place, that would be good, too. It would make Jill happy. With nothing better to do, he took advantage of the free wifi to check his emails. Leaving the message open, he fired up Google Earth and entered the name 'Wildcat Safari'. The software zeroed in, a hodge-podge of squares and colors. Jill slid around the booth's bench to look over his shoulder, her thigh pressed firmly against his. "What's up?" Gardner glanced around. A family was seated in the booth next to theirs, the overweight child complaining to its mother that it wanted a thick shake. A few customers stood at the counter. Nobody else was nearby. Not that anyone would care, but he'd learned you couldn't be too careful. "Cusmano has a cat sanctuary called Wildcat Safari." "Wildcat Safari, huh?" She'd picked up on his caution and kept her voice low. "That's no sanctuary. Not an accredited one, anyway.

I think I've heard Mom talking about it. Yeah." Her lip curled. "I think she said they do big cat hunting. Pay your money and get a chance to shoot a tiger." He tilted his head to look at her. "That's gotta be illegal. Have tigers and lions running around your ranch?" She shook her head slowly, a half smile on her lips. "The cops don't care. Mom says she thinks some of them are involved. Complaints don't work. Provided the fences are secure, it's legal enough. Believe me, we've tried." Gardner tried zooming in on the ranch, but Google Earth couldn't show him any detail. He could sure check its credentials on the web, though. Not listed as an accredited facility. Sold cubs. Visitors by appointment. Call us for a unique hunting experience, stalking deer in our beautiful, forested hills. A few photos of magnificent scenery illustrated the story, along with pictures of the hunting lodge. "It'll be interested to see if this is the same place the cubs came from," Gardner said. And right next to Cusmano's ranch, too. Google Earth showed the buildings, one set out in a U shape, a few out buildings and one large, round building. He wondered what it was. Some sort of garden, or arena? Hard to tell. GARDNER ROLLED THE Jeep back into the mall parking lot at twenty past seven. The rush hour traffic had reduced to a trickle and the shadows were long. If he'd been looking for a parking spot now, he could have had his pick. Most of the bays everywhere but around the entrances were empty. The mall blazed with light, even around the back where the trucks pulled in. One big red semi was on its way out, its engine a low rumble. The van was still there with one of the bays open. A man appeared, carrying a box of what looked like the disassembled boundary fence, which he scooted into one of the big luggage bays underneath. Jill leaned across Gardner so she could see round the corner better. He sucked in a breath, aware of her breasts pressing against him. If she moved a fraction more on his lap, she'd know he was happy to see her. He didn't want that. Not yet, anyway. "They've got cages for the cubs," she said. "Stacked on top of each other." He felt her stiffen. "Bastards." "Steady, Jill." He rubbed her back tentatively. "We're after the

sharks, not the minnows." She sat up and glowered at him. "I hear what you're saying. But meanwhile, the minnows in this case are a bunch of cubs that I'll bet my mother's life aren't much more than six weeks old. By law, they should be at least eight weeks." She tossed her head. "Oh, fuck it. By law. It's bullshit. It shouldn't be allowed. Period." Gardner relaxed. That was one way to disperse his sexual energy. His libido had lost interest. One of the mall security guards jumped down from the loading bay and went around to the big bruiser who had spoken to Gardner in the mall. Gardner's journalist antennae buzzed. What was that about? The bruiser held a box, which he handed to the security guard. The fellow glanced around, then opened the box and examined the contents. Gardner grabbed his camera and zoomed in. Damn. He couldn't see inside. "What are you doing?" Jill asked. "Shut up." The security guard pulled out something. A plastic bag? Unsealed it, put in a finger to taste. Gardner's nerves danced a salsa. "Bingo," he muttered, pressing the shutter. The plastic bag disappeared, the box was sealed. The mall security guard pulled out a long envelope from the inside pocket of his jacket. The bruiser opened the envelope and took out a wad of cash. A lot of cash, judging by the time it took him to count it. Gardner took another photo, and another. The envelope disappeared, the mall guard nodded and walked away, back into the mall with the box. Gardner switched off the camera, a wide grin spreading across his face. Jill stared at him. "What was that?" Leaving the camera on his lap, he pulled Jill forward and kissed her soundly on the lips. She stiffened, recoiling a little. "What?" Keeping a light grip on her arm, he said, "That, my dear, was a drug delivery." Her mouth formed an O. "Are you sure?" "Well now. Let's see what the camera reveals." He sure hoped there had been enough light. Shadows surrounded the pools of light formed by the street lamps. In the west the sky had that pre-sunset orange glow. He displayed the shots in the camera's viewer, showing them to Jill as he did so. "See? The mall guard is tasting something." Jill peered, leaning over him. "Is he? It isn't very clear, is it?" Damn it, no it wasn't very clear, but the computer would do a

better job. He hoped so. "What's happening here? He's checking something?" Jill said. "Counting money." She flicked her eyebrows. "If you say so." The elation drained away like water through a leak. She was right. Neither man's features were clear. He knew who the tiger guard was – had a clear picture of him, but a clever lawyer would laugh at these. Fuck it. He sagged against the seat, his head back. "Don't get me wrong. You're right about the deal. But you'll never prove it with these." A horrible feeling growing in his gut, he opened his eyes and looked at her, her face silhouetted against the sky's orange glow. "Did you ever deal?" An uncomfortable silence grew. "No," she said at last. "I had a boyfriend who tried to get me involved. But I wouldn't. He..." She stopped talking and licked her lips. "I decided to go home." There was a lot she wasn't telling him. Some other time he would have to ask about this boyfriend. Had he beaten her up? Been her pimp? The thought made him feel queasy. Forget about it. One thing at a time. "That's pretty smart, isn't it?" Jill's voice seemed to come from a distance. "Who's going to poke around a place where there are tigers?" He clutched at her words. "Yes, who? Just like Ulysses." He was on the right track.

Chapter 12 ​ SALLY WAS IN THE SHOWER in a motel room when the email came through from Mike Sullivan. He'd spoken to Cusmano, who would love to meet Ash and would be calling soon. Meanwhile, here were the results of the investigation into Cusmano's business activities. Ash opened a spreadsheet with half a dozen closely-annotated sheets leading from one to another. Mike had added a note. 'Since I know you'd want to know about any tiger connections, you'll see on sheet 5 that he has one hundred percent interest through five companies in a tiger sanctuary in North Carolina. It's right next to his holiday home in the Blue Ridge Mountains, a one hundred acre, wooded property he uses for hunting.' A sanctuary? Ash hadn't expected that. Still, it was worth following up. 'Wildcat Safari' didn't sound too much like a sanctuary to him. The page was loading when Sally appeared. God, she was gorgeous, stark naked, slim and strong, her dark hair a curly cloud around her shoulders. She grinned at him from her suitcase. "What're you looking at?" "You. But I'll wait. I had an email from Sullivan. It would appear that Cusmano owns a cat sanctuary." She finished clipping on her bra and pulled the other chair over to sit beside him, running a critical eye over the site's home page. "Is it accredited?" "No." He pointed at an entry down the page. "And you can buy your very own tiger from our award winning breeding stock." The passage was illustrated with a picture of a white tiger cub. "Huh." Sally went back to the suitcase and finished dressing while Ash checked the rest of the spreadsheet. "Clever how he's hidden it through this maze of companies and directorships. I wonder why it's such a secret."

Sally filled the kettle and plugged it in. "Maybe he uses it to hide drugs." Ash sagged back. "Modus operandi, huh?" She finished making tea and brought him back a cup. "Yep." Ash sent an email to Dave Gardner with the name and website address of 'Wildcat Safari'. He'd fulfilled his promise and the journalist could make of it what he wished. Sally had pored over trail maps, looking for places where she might want to take pictures and that was fine with Ash. He drove along the winding mountain roads under the great spruce trees. The pine scent penetrated, soothing his soul. He'd felt the stress roll off him from the time he'd met Sally at the motel near Tiger Territory. He could afford to indulge his lovely wife. After a few more photo stops, Sally declared she was hungry, so Ash found the nearest town on the sat nav. Sally grinned at him as he drove down the main street, two rows of rundown wooden shacks. A dark-skinned man with a white woman? The veranda boards squeaked underfoot and a bell tinkled as they went inside. Dusty shelves of canned and packaged goods stood on one side and a table of fresh vegetables lay on the other. A
